Attachment E - Flight Safety Documents System 
Note. – (Supplementary to Section II, Chapter 1, 1.3) 
1 
Introduction 
1.1 
The following material provides guidance on the organisation and development of an 
operator’s flight safety documents system. It should be understood that the development 
of a flight safety documents system is a complete process, and changes to each 
document comprising the system may affect the entire system. Guidelines applicable to 
the development of operational documents have been produced by government and 
industry sources and are available to operators. Nevertheless, it may be difficult for 
operators to make the best use of these guidelines, since they are distributed across a 
number of publications. 
1.2 
Furthermore, guidelines applicable to operational documents development tend to focus 
on a single aspect of documents design, for example, formatting and typography. 
Guidelines rarely cover the entire process of operational documents development. It is 
important for operational documents to be consistent with each other, and consistent 
with regulations, manufacturer requirements and Human Factors principles. It is also 
necessary to ensure consistency across departments as well as consistency in 
application. Hence the emphasis on an integrated approach, based on the notion of the 
operational documents as a complete system.

scientific research, but also upon current industry best practices, with an emphasis on a 
high degree of operational relevance.

easy access to information required for flight and ground operations contained in the 
various operational documents comprising the system and which facilitate management 
of the distribution and revision of operational documents.

delay the operation if not available in a short time period;

frequently used information; 
d) reference information, e.g. information that is required for the operation but does 
not fall under b) or c) above; and

Section III, Chapter 2, 2.2.1.1, and Chapter 4, 4.11) 
Introduction 
The material in this attachment provides guidance for certified automatic landing systems, 
HUD or equivalent displays and vision systems intended for operational use in helicopters 
engaged in international air navigation. These systems and hybrid systems may be installed 
and operated to reduce workload, improve guidance, reduce flight technical error and enhance 
situational awareness and/or obtain operational credits. Automatic landing systems, HUD or 
equivalent displays and vision systems may be installed separately or together as part of a 
hybrid system. Any operational credit for their use by commercial air transport operators 
requires a specific approval from the CAAM and the State of Registry for general aviation 
operators. 
Note 1.- “Vision systems” is a generic term referring to the existing systems designed to 
provide images, i.e. enhanced vision systems (EVS), synthetic vision systems (SVS) and 
combined vision systems (CVS). 
Note 2.- “Automatic landing system-helicopter” is an automatic approach using airborne 
systems which provide automatic control of the flight path, to a point aligned with the landing

combined vision systems (CVS). 
Note 2.- “Automatic landing system-helicopter” is an automatic approach using airborne 
systems which provide automatic control of the flight path, to a point aligned with the landing 
surface, from which the pilot can transition to a safe landing by means of natural vision without 
the use of automatic control. 
Note 3.- Operational credit can be granted only within the limits of the airworthiness approval. 
Note 4.- Currently, operational credit has been given only to vision systems containing an 
image sensor providing a real-time image of the actual external scene on a HUD. 
Note 5.- More detailed information and guidance on automatic landing systems, HUD or 
equivalent displays and vision systems is contained in the Manual of All-Weather Operations 
(ICAO Doc 9365.) This manual should be consulted in conjunction with this attachment. 
1 
HUD and equivalent displays 
1.1 
General 
1.1.1 A HUD presents flight information into the pilot’s forward external field of view without 
significantly restricting that external view. 
1.1.2 Flight information should be presented on the HUD or an equivalent display, as 
required for the intended use. 
1.2 
Operational applications 
1.2.1 Flight operations with a HUD can improve situational awareness by combining flight 
information located on head-down displays with the external view to provide pilots with 
more immediate awareness of relevant flight parameters and situation information

1.2 
Operational applications 
1.2.1 Flight operations with a HUD can improve situational awareness by combining flight 
information located on head-down displays with the external view to provide pilots with 
more immediate awareness of relevant flight parameters and situation information 
while they continuously view the external scene. This improved situational awareness 
can also reduce errors in flight operations and improve the pilot’s ability to transition 
between instrument and visual references as meteorological conditions change.

1.2.2 A HUD may be used to supplement conventional flight deck instrumentation or as a 
primary flight display if certified for this purpose. 
1.2.3 An approved HUD may: 
a) qualify for operations with reduced visibility or reduced RVR; or 
b) replace some parts of the ground facilities such as touchdown zone and/or centre 
line lights. 
1.2.4 The functions of a HUD may be provided by a suitable equivalent display. However, 
before such systems can be used, the appropriate airworthiness approval should be 
obtained. 
1.3 
HUD training 
Training and recent experience requirements for operations using HUD or equivalent 
displays should, for commercial operators and for general aviation operators be 
established by CAAM. For commercial air transport operations, the training programmes 
should be approved by CAAM and the implementation of the training should be subject 
to oversight by CAAM. The training should address all flight operations for which the 
HUD or the equivalent display is used. 
2 
Vision systems 
2.1 
General 
2.1.1 Vision systems can display electronic real-time images of the actual external scene 
achieved through the use of image sensors, i.e. EVS, or display synthetic images, 
which are derived from the on-board avionic systems, i.e. SVS. Vision systems can 
also consist of a combination of these two systems, called combined vision systems,

achieved through the use of image sensors, i.e. EVS, or display synthetic images, 
which are derived from the on-board avionic systems, i.e. SVS. Vision systems can 
also consist of a combination of these two systems, called combined vision systems, 
i.e. CVS. Such a system may display electronic real-time images of the external scene 
using the EVS component of the system. The information from vision systems may be 
displayed head-up and/or head-down. Operational credit may be granted to vision 
systems which are appropriately qualified. 
2.1.2 Light emitting diode (LED) lights may not be visible to infrared-based vision systems. 
Operators of such vision systems will need to acquire information about the LED 
implementation programmes at aerodromes where they intend to operate. More details 
about the consequences of LED lights are contained in the Manual of All-Weather 
Operations (ICAO Doc 9365). 
2.2 
Operational applications 
2.2.1 Flight operations with EVS allow the pilot to view an image of the external scene 
obscured by darkness or other visibility restrictions. The use of EVS will also allow 
acquisition of an image of the external scene earlier than with natural, unaided vision, 
hence providing for a smoother transition to references by natural vision. The improved 
acquisition of an image of the external scene may improve situational awareness. It 
may also qualify for operational credit if the information from the vision system is

hence providing for a smoother transition to references by natural vision. The improved 
acquisition of an image of the external scene may improve situational awareness. It 
may also qualify for operational credit if the information from the vision system is 
presented to the pilots in a suitable way and the necessary airworthiness approval and 
specific approval by the CAAM have been obtained for the combined system. 
2.2.2 Vision system imagery may also enable pilots to detect other aircraft on the ground, 
terrain or obstructions on or adjacent to runways or taxiways.

2.3 
Operational concepts 
2.3.1 Instrument approach operations include an instrument phase and a visual phase. The 
instrument phase ends at the published MDA/H or DA/H unless a missed approach is 
initiated. Using the EVS or CVS does not change the applicable MDA/H or DA/H. The 
continued approach to landing from MDA/H or DA/H will be conducted using visual 
references. This also applies to operations with vision systems. The difference is that 
the visual references will be acquired by use of an EVS or CVS, natural vision or the 
vision system in combination with natural vision. 
2.3.2 Down to a defined height in the visual segment, typically at or above 30m (100ft), the 
visual references may be acquired solely by means of the vision system. The defined 
height depends on the airworthiness approval and the specific approval by the CAAM. 
Below this height the visual references should be solely based on natural vision. In the 
most advanced applications, the vision system may be used down to touchdown 
without the requirement for natural vision acquisition of visual references. This means 
that such a vision system may be the sole means of acquiring visual references and 
can be used without natural vision.

Hybrid systems 
A hybrid system generically means that two or more systems are combined. The hybrid 
system typically has improved performance compared to each of the component systems, 
which in turn may qualify for operational credit. The inclusion of more systems in the 
hybrid system normally enhances the performance of the system. The Manual of All-
Weather Operations (ICAO Doc 9365) contains some examples of hybrid systems.

in which the term is used, since a change in the meaning of the term would affect the

General 
1.1 
Citation 
1.1.1 
This Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) should be cited as the Civil Aviation Directive 
8302 – Airworthiness Flight Tests and Other Related Flight Tests. 
1.1.2 
This CAD 8302 – Airworthiness Flight Tests and Other Related Flight Tests, Issue 
01/Revision 00 will remain current until withdrawn or superseded. 
1.1.3 
This Directive contains the additional standards, requirements and procedures 
and shall be read together with CAD 8 – Airworthiness of Aircraft. 
1.2 
Applicability 
1.2.1 
The following persons shall be subject to this Directive— 
a) holder of a Permit to Fly issued under MCAR; 
b) the owner of an aircraft; 
c) 
the lessee of an aircraft; 
d) pilots approved in accordance with paragraph 2.4 below; 
e) an approved maintenance organisation issued by the CAAM; and 
f) 
an organisation that is approved to manage continuing airworthiness. 
1.2.2 
CAAM may require airworthiness flight tests or other related flight tests to be 
performed in support of initial or continuing airworthiness assurance. 
1.3 
Revocation 
1.3.1 
CAD 8301 – Certificate of Airworthiness with this CAD, revokes Airworthiness 
Notice No. 45 - Airworthiness Flight Test, Issue 4 dated 15 May 2005. 
1.4 
Definitions  
1.4.1 
In this Directive, unless the context otherwise requires— 
Airworthiness Flight Test Schedule means a planned flight testing form that details

Notice No. 45 - Airworthiness Flight Test, Issue 4 dated 15 May 2005. 
1.4 
Definitions  
1.4.1 
In this Directive, unless the context otherwise requires— 
Airworthiness Flight Test Schedule means a planned flight testing form that details 
numerous ground and flight tests to be accomplished. 
Airworthiness Flight Test Report means a report which details the ground and flight 
test results and is a prerequisite for consideration for Malaysian certificate of 
airworthiness.

Airworthiness Flight Test Schedule (AFTS) 
2.1 
Development of AFTS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2.1.1 
The AFTS shall be prepared by the Continuing Airworthiness Management 
Organisation (CAMO) and submitted together with a completed Statement of 
Compliance (SOC) (CAAM/AW/8101-01) and supporting Flight Test related 
documents, for example, manufacturer’s flight test schedule to enable CAAM to 
review and approve the AFTS.  
Note. – Any AFTS that are generic in nature i.e. not applicable to specific aircraft   
types, for example, CAA UK’s AFTS applicable for single, piston-engine 
aeroplanes up to 2730 kg (6000 lb) MTOM and other equivalent AFTS, can be 
used by CAMO ‘as-is’ and does not require CAAM Airworthiness Division’s 
approval. 
2.1.2 
Upon satisfactory review of the CAMO’s submitted AFTS, CAAM may approve the 
AFTS by endorsing both the Statement of Compliance (SOC) and the cover page 
of the CAMO’s AFTS. 
2.1.3 
When an imported used aircraft is acceptable to CAAM and issued with a 
Malaysian Certificate of Registration, the subject used aircraft may be flight tested 
using CAAM approved AFTS and under the conditions of a Malaysian issued 
Permit to Fly (PtF). 
2.1.4 
Alternatively, a used aircraft may be flight tested under an exporting foreign 
registration provided the following are fulfilled—

using CAAM approved AFTS and under the conditions of a Malaysian issued 
Permit to Fly (PtF). 
2.1.4 
Alternatively, a used aircraft may be flight tested under an exporting foreign 
registration provided the following are fulfilled—  
a) agreement between the existing foreign owner and the new Malaysian owner 
on the terms of responsibilities for the Airworthiness Flight Test, which 
includes the involvement of CAAM approved CAMO; 
b) conduct of Airworthiness Flight Test per CAAM approved AFTS; 
c) 
the subject aircraft’s documents like certificate of airworthiness, certificate of 
registration, aircraft flight manual, aircraft radio licence, third party liability 
insurance certificate, mass & balance document and passenger and/or cargo 
manifests (if applicable) are valid; 
d) the subject aircraft is declared as airworthy prior to the Airworthiness Flight 
Test; 
e) the pilot-in-command for the Airworthiness Flight Test has valid pilot’s flying 
licence with appropriate type rating(s); 
f) 
the Malaysian owner’s flight crew or equivalent shall be the observer for the 
Airworthiness Flight Test and is responsible for the acceptance of the used 
aircraft into Malaysia’s aircraft register;

g) the existing foreign owner shall ensure that any defects encountered during 
the Airworthiness Flight Test are recorded and rectified accordingly and

h) the CAMO engaged by the Malaysian owner is responsible for the preparation 
of the used aircraft’s Airworthiness Flight Test Report and its submission for 
CAAM’s acceptance; and 
i) 
the CAMO engaged by the Malaysian owner shall provide the above-
mentioned proposal for CAAM’s acceptance. 
2.2 
Amendment to AFTS 
2.2.1 
Amendments to the AFTS shall be submitted together with a new SOC as well as 
supporting Flight Test related documents for CAAM’s review and approval. Copies 
of previously approved AFTS and its associated SOC shall be submitted too. 
2.2.2 
Upon satisfactory review of the CAMO’s amended AFTS, CAAM may approve the 
AFTS by endorsing both the SOC and cover page of the CAMO’s AFTS.  
2.3 
Contents of the AFTS 
2.3.1 
The CAMO’s AFTS shall contain the following—  
a) AFTS reference number, issue number and date; 
b) Policies/ Procedures in respect of Minimum Flight Test Crew including 
Carriage of Passengers during Test Flight, Aircraft Flight Manual limitations 
and Approved Pilots for Flight Test; 
Note. – Aircraft Flight Manual limitations shall not be exceeded during the test flight 
or the Permit to Fly may be invalidated. 
c)

Carriage of Passengers during Test Flight, Aircraft Flight Manual limitations 
and Approved Pilots for Flight Test; 
Note. – Aircraft Flight Manual limitations shall not be exceeded during the test flight 
or the Permit to Fly may be invalidated. 
c) 
Flight Test Certificate or equivalent; 
d) Flights conducted with valid Permit to Fly (PtF) or equivalent; 
e) Mandatory placards/ markings checking; 
f) 
Defects encountered during the test flight and their rectifications;  
g) Individual tests, for example, one engine inoperative climb test, low speed 
handling test, autorotation test, power assurance test, stall test, dive to never-
exceed speed test, aircraft’s system(s) test(s), etc; and 
h) Load sheet.Airworthiness Flight Test 
2.4 
Approval of Pilots to Carry Out Airworthiness Flight Test 
 
 
  
2.4.1 
CAMO shall nominate pilots who are properly qualified with adequate flying 
experience to carry out Airworthiness Flight Test. The pilot’s flying experience 
requirements shall be as per paragraph 3.1.2. The CAAM may approve the 
nominated pilots.

2.4.2 
The minimum experience required to carry flight test are as follows─  
a) AEROPLANE ≤ 5,700 kg. 
1) A minimum of 400 hours total flying time for single-engine aircraft, or 800 
hours total flying time, including a minimum of 100 hours on light twin engine 
aircraft as pilot in command, for twin-engine aircraft; and 
2) Recent experience on the particular aircraft type or similar aircraft types, 
amounting to at least 10 hours in the last 12 months for single-engine aircraft 
and 20 hours in the last 12 months for twin-engine aircraft: and 
3) Familiarity with, and in current spinning practice for, testing of aircraft 
certified for spinning. 
b) HELICOPTER 
1) A minimum of 400 hours total flying time for single-engine helicopters, or 800 
hours total flying time for twin-engine helicopters; and 
2) Recent experience on the particular helicopter type or, for single engine 
helicopters below 2,730 kg, similar helicopter types, amounting to at least 
20 hours in the last 12 months. 
c) 
AEROPLANE > 5,700 kg. 
1) Recent experience on the particular aircraft type, amounting to at least 50 
hours in the last 12 months, and are designated as CAAM Authorised 
Examiners. 
Note. – When a pilot does not meet the above requirements, the CAAM may 
accept if they are appropriately type rated professional test pilots or

hours in the last 12 months, and are designated as CAAM Authorised 
Examiners. 
Note. – When a pilot does not meet the above requirements, the CAAM may 
accept if they are appropriately type rated professional test pilots or 
appropriately type rated flying instructors. CAAM may also accept 
applications from sole owners of aircraft up to 2730 kg MTOW provided 
he/she is type rated on the subject aircraft. 
2.4.3 
CAMO shall complete CAAM’s application form Pilot’s application to conduct 
Airworthiness Flight Test (CAAM/AW/8302-04) and submit to CAAM Airworthiness 
Division.  
2.4.4 
Prior to initial approval, Pilots intending to carry out Airworthiness Flight Test shall 
be briefed by CAAM on the safety precautions and flight test techniques. 
2.4.5 
After the briefing, CAAM may fly together with the pilot to complement the briefing. 
2.4.6 
When above Paragraphs 3.1.1 to 3.1.5 are satisfactorily completed, CAAM shall 
approve the pilot concerned. 
2.5 
Insurance Cover for Airworthiness Flight Tests 
2.5.1 
When the Airworthiness Flight Test involves any CAAM personnel, the CAMO 
shall ensure that each CAAM personnel is provided insurance coverage against

all air risks. This insurance coverage for CAAM personnel shall be at par with the 
Aircraft Operator’s Flight Crew insurance coverage. 
2.6 
Post Flight Procedures and Aircraft Performance Analysis 
2.6.1 
Upon completion of the Airworthiness Flight Test, the pilot shall record in the Flight 
Test Certificate, as well as, in the Journey Log any defects arising from the Flight 
Test. If a re-flight test is required, the pilot shall ensure all tests are completed. 
2.6.2 
The pilot shall ensure that all flight test results are available and properly recorded. 
2.6.3 
The pilot shall ensure that the aircraft’s performance analysis is completed and 
compared with the Aircraft Flight Manual’s performance data. If the aircraft’s 
performance is found to be worse when compared with the Aircraft Flight Manual, 
the pilot shall record in the Flight Test Certificate, as well as, in the Journey Log 
for CAMO’s corrective action. 
2.6.4 
If a qualified Airworthiness Engineer or Aircraft Maintenance Engineer is part of 
the Aircraft Operator’s Airworthiness Flight Test Team, this Engineer shall ensure 
that the flight test results including aircraft’s performance analysis are complete 
and properly recorded. 
2.7 
Post Flight Reporting 
2.7.1 
The CAMO shall ensure the Airworthiness Flight Test Report is completed

that the flight test results including aircraft’s performance analysis are complete 
and properly recorded. 
2.7 
Post Flight Reporting 
2.7.1 
The CAMO shall ensure the Airworthiness Flight Test Report is completed 
satisfactorily prior to submission to CAAM Airworthiness Division. Any incomplete 
or unsatisfactory Airworthiness Flight Test Report submitted may be rejected and 
the aircraft may be subjected to another flight test. 
2.7.2 
The CAMO shall submit the following together with the Airworthiness Flight Test 
Report—  
a) Load Sheet; 
b) Achieved/ Actual Performance Climb Graph; 
c) 
Scheduled Performance Climb calculations including Flight Manual’s climb 
graph/ chart; 
d) Scheduled Stall calculations including Flight Manual’s stall graph/ chart; 
e) Power Assurance Checks calculations including Flight Manual’s power 
assurance graph/ chart (for helicopters); 
f) 
Autorotation Checks calculations including autorotation graph/ chart (for 
helicopters); and 
g) Aircraft defects encountered during Airworthiness Flight Test and their 
rectifications.

Other Related Flight Tests 
3.1 
Flight Test Due to Manufacturer’s Maintenance Requirements 
 
3.1.1 
If maintenance check flight is required by the aircraft maintenance manual or any 
other maintenance data issued by the design approval holder being responsible 
for continuing airworthiness of the aircraft, CAMO may accurately transcribe the 
applicable maintenance data to develop its own Maintenance Check Flight 
Schedule (MCFS) in accordance with procedures in CAAM-approved CAME. The 
MCFS is not required to be approved by CAAM unless there is deviation from the 
aforementioned maintenance data. 
3.1.2 
The Flight Test Schedule (FTS) shall be prepared by the CAMO and submitted 
together with a completed SOC and supporting Flight Test related documents to 
CAAM. 
3.1.3 
Upon satisfactory review of the CAMO’s submitted FTS, CAAM may approve the 
FTS by endorsing the SOC and the cover page of the CAMO’s FTS.  
3.1.4 
The CAMO’s FTS shall contain the following—  
a) FTS reference number, issue number and date; 
b) Policies/ Procedures in respect of Minimum Flight Test Crew including 
Carriage of Passengers during Test Flight, Aircraft Flight Manual limitations 
and appropriate type rated Pilots to conduct the Flight Test; 
Note. – Aircraft Flight Manual limitations shall not be exceeded during the Test 
Flight or the Permit to Fly may be invalidated. 
c)

Carriage of Passengers during Test Flight, Aircraft Flight Manual limitations 
and appropriate type rated Pilots to conduct the Flight Test; 
Note. – Aircraft Flight Manual limitations shall not be exceeded during the Test 
Flight or the Permit to Fly may be invalidated. 
c) 
Flight Test Certificate or equivalent; 
d) Flights conducted with valid Permit to Fly (PtF);  
e) Defects encountered during the test flight and their rectifications; and 
f) 
Load sheet. 
3.2 
Post Flight Procedures 
3.2.1 
Upon completion of the Flight Test 
The pilot shall record in the Flight Test Certificate, as well as, in the Journey Log 
any defects arising from the flight test. If a re-flight test is required, the pilot shall 
ensure all affected areas are completed. 
3.2.2 
After the Flight Test 
The pilot shall ensure that all test results are available and properly recorded 
3.2.3 
Records

After the Flight Test, the CAMO shall ensure that the Airworthiness Flight Test 
Report including associated maintenance actions are documented and kept as 
part of aircraft maintenance records.  
 
3.3 
Flight Test Due to Modification(s) or Repair(s) 
3.3.1 
When an aircraft modification or repair requires Flight Test via compliance to type 
certification or supplement type certification requirements, these Flight Test(s) 
shall be carried out in accordance with manufacturer’s requirements as well as the 
following requirements—  
a) nomination of Test Pilot (modification/ repair) according to paragraph 3.1; and 
b) submission of Flight Test Plan including supporting documents for CAAM’s 
approval/acceptance. 
 
 
CAMO’s AFT Policies and Procedures Interface with CAAM 
4.1 
Policies and procedures 
4.1.1 
CAME shall contain policies and procedures on Aircraft Flight Test with respect to 
compliance to this directive. 
4.2 
CAAM participation 
4.2.1 
CAAM may participate in CAMO’s airworthiness flight test as and when required.  
4.3 
Downgrading 
4.3.1 
If a CAMO’s aircraft shows signs of degrading performance i.e. aircraft 
performance is not able meet the Aircraft Flight Manual’s performance data, the 
aircraft may be subject to performance downgrade by CAAM.

PREFACE 
 
 
BACKGROUND 
 
 
Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, published in 1999, contains the rules, 
procedures and guidance material applicable to all Air Traffic Services units. 
 
To ensure efficient provision of air traffic services at regional, local or unit levels, 
operational instructions in the form of ROIs, SOIs and UOIs are issued, either by ATS 
HQ or by local units. Over the years, the various units have accumulated numerous 
instructions that are still current. 
 
Hence, there was a definite need to publish a manual incorporating the numerous ROIs, 
SOIs and UOIs into a single document. This manual hereby referred to as Manual of Air 
Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 2, contains directives and instructions which are 
applicable on a regional or local basis as appropriate. 
 
 
CONSISTENCY WITH MATS VOLUME 1 
 
 
Units issuing instructions shall make every effort to ensure that the instructions do not 
contravene any rule, procedure or guidance material found in MATS Volume 1. In the 
event that any instruction is found to contravene MATS Volume 1, the Unit Head shall 
be notified immediately. However, until such time an amendment is made, the 
instruction in MATS Volume 2 shall still apply. 
 
Whilst repetition of instruction readily available in other documents is not encouraged, it

be notified immediately. However, until such time an amendment is made, the 
instruction in MATS Volume 2 shall still apply. 
 
Whilst repetition of instruction readily available in other documents is not encouraged, it 
is permitted to ensure clarity. In other circumstances, reference to other instructions or 
documents will suffice.

FORMAT 
 
 
This volume is divided into several Parts. With the exception of Subang ATCC, each 
airport that is manned by ATC personnel is allocated a Part. Each Part is sub-divided into 
numbered Section headings in bold, each dealing with a particular subject. Where the 
subjects have been expanded or qualified, numbered sub-headings in bold are used. All 
text and graphics under the subject heading and sub-headings belongs to that main 
subject heading. 
 
Aside from Section heading and sub-headings, certain sentences or paragraphs will be 
highlighted in bold for emphasis. 
 
OPERATIONAL INSTRUCTIONS ISSUED AFTER THE PUBLICATION OF MATS 
VOLUME 2 
 
From time to time, new operational instructions will be issued. These instructions may be 
of a permanent or temporary nature. To ensure that the controllers concerned are aware 
of the changes, these instructions shall be in the form of UOIs, ROIs or SOIs. Those 
operational instructions of a permanent nature shall be incorporated into the appropriate 
parts of this Volume as soon as possible whereas those of a temporary nature shall be 
self-cancelling. 
 
GENDER NEUTRAL 
 
 
The pronouns “he”, “him” and “his” when used are for convenience and such they are 
gender neutral.

CHAPTER 2 - CONTROLLER’S DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITY 
 
 
SECTION 1 – GENERAL 
 
1.1 
This part defines the duties and responsibilities of controllers working at Subang 
Tower. Controllers shall read this part in conjunction with MATS Vol. 1, PART 1, 
SECTION 1 – ATS ADMINISTRATION which amongst others defines in general 
terms the responsibilities of controllers. Controller specific responsibilities and 
actions associated with provision of ATS are defined in other Parts of this MATS 
Vol. 2. 
 
1.2 
During HOW/TOW, Controllers shall ensure the following information is included 
in the verbal briefing: 
 
a) runway mode. 
b) departure clearance. 
c) departure frequency. 
d) traffic situation. 
e) closed area. 
f) airspace restriction. 
g) equipment status. 
h) weather condition; and 
i) any other pertinent information. 
 
1.3 
Chain - of - Command 
 
1.3.1 Under normal circumstances, there will be six (6) operational controllers at the 
Tower. The Tower Supervisor shall be the officer responsible for the general 
operation of the Tower. 
 
1.3.2 Abnormal circumstances, e.g. aircraft on emergency, may, require the presence 
of additional rated controllers including the CAAM Manager. During such 
situations, the “chain - of – command” shall be as follows: 
 
a) CAAM Manager.

operation of the Tower. 
 
1.3.2 Abnormal circumstances, e.g. aircraft on emergency, may, require the presence 
of additional rated controllers including the CAAM Manager. During such 
situations, the “chain - of – command” shall be as follows: 
 
a) CAAM Manager. 
b) Rostered Tower Supervisor. 
c) Rostered Aerodrome Controllers (ADC). 
d) Rostered Surface Movement Controller (SMC). 
e) Rostered ADC Assistant.

SECTION 2 – ATS LOG PROCEDURES 
 
2.1 
Introduction 
 
2.1.1 An ATS logbook is a record of all significant occurrences and actions relating to 
operations, facilities, equipment, and staff. 
 
2.1.2 As stipulated in MATS Vol.1 Part 1, Para 1.7, controllers are to log down any 
significant occurrences in tower logbook 
 
2.2 
Logbook Procedures 
 
2.2.1 Tower shall maintain two logbooks, each for odd and even days. Recording will 
start at 0000 UTC and end at 2359 UTC each day 
 
2.2.2 Any controller may make an entry, but all entries shall be made in an indelible 
manner and no erasure is permitted. Incorrect information shall be struck out and 
correct information inserted and initialled (controller’s operating initial). 
 
2.2.3 An entry shall have sufficient details of the aircraft or flight, vehicle and personnel 
involved. Sufficient details will give readers a full understanding for a better and 
comprehensive follow up action 
 
2.2.4 The letter ‘LE’ shall be used to indicate a late entry log 
 
2.2.5 All entries shall be initialled with controller’s operating initial. (Ref MATS Vol II 
Appendix A) 
 
2.2.6 An entry that needs to be brought forward for the attention of management shall 
be annotated to enable the manager, deputy manager or assistant manager to 
take follow up action

2.2.5 All entries shall be initialled with controller’s operating initial. (Ref MATS Vol II 
Appendix A) 
 
2.2.6 An entry that needs to be brought forward for the attention of management shall 
be annotated to enable the manager, deputy manager or assistant manager to 
take follow up action 
 
2.2.7 CAAM Subang Manager or Deputy Manager or Assistant Manager shall review 
the log entries at least once each working day and acknowledge by initial and date 
 
2.2.8 If the logbook needs to be impounded for the purposes of an inquiry, replacement 
logbook shall be provided. These actions shall be recorded in both current and 
replacement logbook 
 
2.2.9 Logbooks will be replaced on the first day of the year 
 
2.3 
Recovery Plan 
 
2.3.1 In the situation where logbook was found to be lost or destroyed due to any reason, 
a replacement logbook shall be provided. These actions shall be recorded in the 
replacement logbook

SECTION 3 - DIVISION OF DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITY 
 
3.1 
Tower Supervisor (ET Position) 
 
3.1.1 Tower Supervisor shall be responsible for: 
a) the efficiency of the control tower in accordance with relevant provisions 
b) directing the work of other ATC personnel under his charge 
c) supervising the training of Tower personnel 
d) coordinating with units providing maintenance, crash and rescue services when 
the need arises 
e) Informing Controllers of new Instruction/Circulars and any changes in 
procedure. 
f) Record any fault/irregularity/changes/status of facilities, equipment, 
g) Provide assistance at any workstation position when required by supervising, 
in particular during distress/emergency and/or security connected situation, the 
controller actions. 
h) Ensure all working position are manned 
i) Verify and provide accurate information in Daily Briefing Format 
 
 
3.2 
Subang ADC (EU Position) 
 
3.2.1 Subang ADC shall be responsible for providing a safe, orderly and expeditiously 
flow of air traffic on and in the vicinity of WMSA with the objective of preventing 
collisions between: 
a) aircraft flying in the aerodrome traffic circuit and 
b) aircraft operating on the active Runway and the entry / exit points 
 
3.2.2 He shall also be responsible for:

flow of air traffic on and in the vicinity of WMSA with the objective of preventing 
collisions between: 
a) aircraft flying in the aerodrome traffic circuit and 
b) aircraft operating on the active Runway and the entry / exit points 
 
3.2.2 He shall also be responsible for: 
a) rendering all possible assistance to aircraft in emergency or distress; and 
b) providing aircraft with meteorological and other information required for the safe 
and efficient conduct of flight. 
c) inform and/or coordinate with other position and/or unit in case of any 
situation/irregularity if necessary. 
d) training of controller on that position 
 
3.3 
Subang SMC (EV Position) 
 
3.3.1 Subang SMC shall be responsible for providing a safe, orderly and expeditiously 
flow of air traffic with the objective of preventing collisions on manoeuvring area, 
except the active Runway and the entry / exit points between: 
a) aircraft and aircraft. 
b) aircraft and vehicles. 
c) aircraft and obstructions on that area. 
 
3.3.2 He shall also be responsible for: 
a) operation of aerodrome ground lighting 
b) inform and/or coordinate with other position and/or unit in case of any 
situation/irregularity if necessary. 
c) training of controller on that position.

SECTION 7 - INFRINGEMENT REPORTING FOR GROUND OPERATIONS AT 
SUBANG AIRPORT 
 
7.1 
Introduction 
7.1.1 The procedure has been designed as part of safety measure to address safety 
issues such as infringements, breaches of rules and non-standard practices by 
ground operations in Subang airport. 
 
7.1.2 The objective of procedure is to improve the level of flight safety not only from the 
lesson learned from reported incidents and any subsequent follow-up action but 
also to alert Subang Aviation community of such unsafe activities. 
 
7.1.3 The objective of this requirement to report infringements is not to determine or 
apportion any blame or liability in connection with any unsafe aviation occurrences 
at Subang airport. 
 
7.1.4 The UOI is being issued to address immediately any safety issues involving 
Subang Airport Ground Operations. Other incidents involving aircraft shall be 
reported in accordance with the mandatory Occurrence Reporting Scheme 
procedures promulgated by Flight Operation Division of CAAM and the reporting 
requirements laid out in Manual of Air Traffic Services Malaysia. 
 
7.2 
Reportable Occurrence 
7.2.1 A reportable incident involving ground operations means any incident relating to 
an aircraft operation, which if not corrected, would endanger the aircraft and/or its

requirements laid out in Manual of Air Traffic Services Malaysia. 
 
7.2 
Reportable Occurrence 
7.2.1 A reportable incident involving ground operations means any incident relating to 
an aircraft operation, which if not corrected, would endanger the aircraft and/or its 
occupants and any other aircraft or person, such as towing activities that don’t 
follow procedures or breach of ATC instructions. 
 
7.2.2 A report should also be submitted on any occurrences which did not actually 
endanger the aircraft, but which if allowed to continue uncorrected or which, if 
repeated in different circumstances, could create a hazard, for example, a 
defective condition, unsatisfactory behavior or faulty procedures.

SECTION 5 – AUTO LAUNCH 
 
5.1 
Auto Launch Procedure 
 
 
a) Only for RWY 15 when mode of operation at KLIA is on RWY 32/33 
configuration. For reciprocal RWY 33 departure, Subang Tower still requires a 
‘Next-Off’ clearance from Lumpur Approach. 
 
b) Spacing between departures minimum of 3 minutes with same performance or 
following is slower succeeding aircraft. 
 
c) If succeeding traffic is faster, Subang ADC shall observe the last vacated 
altitude of the preceding aircraft, establish adequate vertical separation before 
launching the following traffic. 
 
d) Northeast direction – departures from RWY15 making a left turn, Subang Tower 
shall transfer the departure to NEH (118.65 MHz). 
 
e) Southerly direction – departures from RWY15 making a right turn shall be 
transferred by Subang Tower to NWH (124.2 MHz). 
 
f) North / North West direction - departures from RWY15 making a right turn shall 
be transferred by Subang Tower to NWH. 
 
g) Subang ADC should be aware of the new missed approach procedure. Aircraft 
carrying out a missed approach may not be separated with aircraft holding at 
downwind or west of the airfield. 
 
h) Subang ADC shall manage any conflicts or coordinate with Lumpur Approach 
for a non-standard missed approach manoeuvre.

5.3 
Suspension of Auto Launch 
 
When traffic warrants due to the following reasons, Lumpur Approach will inform 
Subang Tower to temporarily suspend the auto launch: 
a) Bad weather with too many aircraft deviating. 
b) Heavy workload at Approach Sector. 
c) Degrading in communication or surveillance facilities.

opting to full suspension. Lumpur Approach shall advise Subang Tower in a timely manner 
when auto launch RWY 15 can be resumed.

SECTION 11 - PROVISION OF ASSISTANCE TO VFR TRAFFIC THAT 
ENCOUNTER NAVIGATIONAL DIFFICULTIES AND ARE 
LOST 
 
11.1 
Introduction 
 
VFR traffic may encounter navigational difficulties and may be lost in both in visual 
meteorological conditions or instrument meteorological conditions. It would be 
impossible to predict the precise the nature of response from air traffic control as 
the actual situations in each scenario may vary. 
 
11.2 
Guideline 
 
The following is a general guideline to help an air traffic controller makes the 
appropriate decision in handling such an abnormal situation. 
 
a) Classification 
VFR traffic that is lost shall be classified as aircraft in difficulty or under 
emergency based on the judgment of the air traffic controller and is dependent 
on the situation. 
 
b) Aircraft in difficulty 
A pilot may still be in normal control of his aircraft and able to follow ATC 
instructions or advisory to regain navigational capability with the assistance of

emergency based on the judgment of the air traffic controller and is dependent 
on the situation. 
 
b) Aircraft in difficulty 
A pilot may still be in normal control of his aircraft and able to follow ATC 
instructions or advisory to regain navigational capability with the assistance of 
ATC such as radar vectors while maintaining safe altitudes. This may be 
considered as an aircraft in difficulty until recovery of navigational 
independence. 
 
c) Aircraft under emergency 
VFR traffic in difficult weather, below safe altitudes which affect safe flight may 
be considered as an aircraft in emergency. Aircraft and occupants may be

d) Recognition 
Due to workload and other in-flight situations, pilot may forget to declare PAN 
or MAYDAY. Despite this, other verbal commentaries by pilot may indicate that 
he may be facing a difficult situation. It is important that controllers recognize 
the situations as early as possible to provide the necessary assistance. A query 
from the controller to the pilot if he intends to declare a PAN or MAYDAY may 
help clarify the situation for both pilot and controller. 
 
e) Coordination 
Coordination with other relevant units for assistance requires accurate 
communications of the situation. Inaccurate choice of words describing the 
scenario and the type of assistance required may elicit the wrong response and 
mishandling of the situation. Use of the key words such as ‘aircraft in difficulty’ 
or ‘emergency’ will elicit an urgent response rather than the words such as 
‘requesting’, ‘require assistance’. The words request ‘IFR’ and request ‘radar 
vectors’ carry different meaning and circumstances. 
 
f) Priority 
Priority handling of aircraft in difficulty must be recognized and enforced to 
prevent deterioration of the situation. This includes ignoring non-priority

vectors’ carry different meaning and circumstances. 
 
f) Priority 
Priority handling of aircraft in difficulty must be recognized and enforced to 
prevent deterioration of the situation. This includes ignoring non-priority 
coordination, curbing non-priority transmissions, transfer of non-priority traffic 
to adjacent units and when possible, calling for assistance from other ATC 
personnel. 
 
g) Frequency 
In-flight situation sometimes can prevent emergency aircraft from switching 
frequencies to other units. In such circumstance’s controllers, should explore 
the possibility of maintaining traffic concerned on the current frequency and 
relaying the necessary instructions. 
 
h) Confidence building 
In-flight situation of aircraft in difficulty or emergency can be one of stress and 
despair. An accommodating and helpful voice and will help smooth the rough 
situation and build confidence instead of irritated commands and scolding by 
air traffic controllers.

i) Radar Vector Assistance 
MATS Volume 1 Part 8 authorizes controllers to vector VFR aircraft provided 
the aircraft request it or it is suggested by the controller and the aircraft accepts 
it. When vectoring VFR aircraft controllers shall take into consideration the 
surrounding terrain near the aircraft concerned before assigning or suggesting 
an altitude. This includes prevailing weather conditions so as to avoid heading 
the aircraft into IMC. Controllers shall exercise caution when vectoring a VFR 
aircraft as the pilot may be inexperienced and be confused easily.

SECTION 15 - MISSED APPROACH PROCEDURE 
 
15.1 
Runway 15 
 
15.1.1 ILS or LOC Approach & NDB Approach 
Proceed on track 149o climbing initially to 2000ft. Passing 1000ft, not before 15.8 
NM VBA DME, turn right (IAS MAX 210 KT) on TR 320°. Crossing RDL 195 VBA 
continue climb to 3000 ft; reaching 3000 ft turn left bound to RUKVU M.A. Holding 
pattern. 
 
15.1.2 RNAV (GNSS) Approach 
Climb to 2000ft, proceed to SA402 on TR149°, at SA402 (1500ft or above) turn 
right (IAS max 210kt) to SA403 (maintain 2000ft), at SA403 turn right to SA404, at 
SA404 climb to 3000ft proceed to SA405 (maintain 3000ft), at SA405 turn left to 
RUKVU or as directed by ATC. 
 
15.2 
Runway 33 
 
15.2.1 RNAV (GNSS) Approach 
At missed approach point / OCA, climb to 3300ft, proceed to CE (maintain 3300ft) 
on TR329° or as directed by ATC. 
 
Note: Subang ADC should aware that aircraft carrying out a missed approach may not be separated 
with aircraft holding at downwind or west of the airfield

Go Around

a) Inform, by use of the HOT LINE, the APP controller responsible for providing a 
departure that a missed approach has occurred; 
b) Coordinate with the APP controller to establish separation with any conflicting 
traffic.

Between Departing Aircraft 
 
 
16.1.1 “Next-Off” Departures

16.1.2 “Auto-Launch” Departures 
 
 
Refer “Auto-Launch” Procedure Para 4.1

preceding VFR departure and VFR aircraft operating in the vicinity of the airport. 
 
16.2 
Between IFR Arrivals and VFR Arrivals including circuit traffic 
 
 
Subang ADC and Lumpur Approach shall be jointly responsible to ensure that 
timely coordination is affected so that an orderly sequence is established. 
 
16.3 
Between Arriving and Departing Aircraft 
 
 
16.3.1 Subang ADC shall clear an arriving aircraft to land only when there is assurance 
that the preceding departing aircraft is airborne before the landing aircraft crosses 
the beginning of the runway on its final approach. 
 
16.3.2 The decision to release an aircraft ahead of an arriving aircraft is dependent on 
several factors, e.g., the distance to touchdown of the arrival, wake turbulence, 
weather conditions, the departing aircraft type, the track after take-off, the flight 
crew, etc.

CHAPTER 4 - EMERGENCY PROCEDURES 
SECTION 1 - GENERAL 
1.1 
Objective 
1.1.1 Emergency procedures are designed to ensure effective coordination amongst 
participating authorities in responding to an aircraft emergency occurring at the 
airport or in its vicinity. The objective is to minimize the effects of an emergency, 
particular in respect of saving lives and maintaining aircraft operation. 
 
1.2 
Airport Emergency Committee 
1.2.1 
The Airport Emergency Committee comprises of representative from the following 
agencies: 
a) Malaysia Airports Sdn Bhd (MASB) 
b) Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) 
c) Medical/Health Departure. (Pusat Perubatan Universiti Malaya / Hospital 
Tengku Ampuan Rahimah / Hospital Besar Kuala Lumpur) 
d) Polis Di Raja Malaysia (Kg Subang / Petaling Jaya) 
e) Jabatan Bomba dan Penyelamat Malaysia (JBPM) 
f) Royal Malaysian Air Force 
g) Red Crescent Society 
h) Angkatan Pertahanan Awam Malaysia (APM) 
i) Telekom Malaysia (Airport) 
j) Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) 
k) Syarikat Bekalan Air Selangor (SYABAS) 
l) Pos Malaysia 
m) Airline / Aircraft Operators 
n) Royal Malaysian Navy (Pelabuhan Kelang) 
o) Kastam Di Raja Malaysia (Cawangan Pencegah Laut) 
p) Klang Port Commission (Safety and Security) 
q) Jabatan Laut Selangor 
 
 
1.3 
Delegation of Responsibility

l) Pos Malaysia

n) Royal Malaysian Navy (Pelabuhan Kelang)

the course of an accident/incident, then the next senior official in the 
agency/department, his deputy shall assume his/her functions and duties. This 
delegation of duties shah be (in alphabetical order) as follows:

1.4 
Site of Emergency 
 
 
a) Aircraft Crash on Airport 
Aircraft incident/accident in the Critical Rescue and Fire Fighting Access Area 
(CRFFAA) which is a rectangular area surrounding the runway. Its width extends 
150m outward each side of the runway centerline, and its length 1000m beyond 
each threshold. 
b) Aircraft Crash off Airport 
Aircraft incident/accident in the area outside the aerodrome perimeter within a 
distance of approximately 8km (5NM) from the centre of the airport. Aircraft 
crash off airport also includes aircraft incident/accident in the area beyond the 
distance of 8km from the centre of the airport. 
 
1.5 
Degree of Response 
The degree of response by Emergency Services is dependent on the category of 
the emergency. The categories of emergency include: 
a) Aircraft in difficulty – Local standby. 
b) Full Emergency – Imminent Crash. 
c) Full Emergency – Land Crash. 
d) Bomb Threat to aircraft

1.5 
Degree of Response 
The degree of response by Emergency Services is dependent on the category of 
the emergency. The categories of emergency include: 
a) Aircraft in difficulty – Local standby. 
b) Full Emergency – Imminent Crash. 
c) Full Emergency – Land Crash. 
d) Bomb Threat to aircraft 
e) Aircraft Subject to Hijack 
 
 
1.6 
Initial Action 
 
 
1.6.1 
If an aircraft emergency is detected, air traffic control, or the first person becoming 
aware of the situation shall initiate the applicable procedure. 
1.6.2 
An emergency phase may be upgraded at the discretion of Duty Controller or the 
AFRS Officer-In-Charge as and when the need arises.

1.6.3 
Emergency response to an aircraft crash outside the Airport Boundary but within 8 
km of the Airport, will be the same as for an aircraft crash on the Airport. The AFRS 
Officer-In-Charge will determine the emergency response to an aircraft crash 
outside of 8 km from the Airport. 
 
1.6.4 
Aeronautical Rescue Coordination Centre (ARCC)/Aeronautical Rescue Sub 
Centre(ARSC) shall be activated even though the accident is being coordinated 
under Airport Emergency Plan in order to facilitate assistance whenever required. 
 
 
SECTION 2 - TYPE OF EMERGENCY AND DEFINITION 
 
There are three types of Aircraft Emergency phase, classified as follows: 
a) Aircraft In Difficulty – Local Standby 
An aircraft in flight known or suspected to have developed some defect but the 
trouble is not such as would normally involve any serious difficulty in effecting a 
safe landing. 
 
b) Full Emergency – Imminent Crash 
An aircraft in flight known or suspected to be in difficulty which may result in a 
force landing or crash on or in the vicinity of the aerodrome. 
 
c) Full Emergency – Land Crash 
Aircraft crash with or without fire which has occurred on or in the vicinity of the 
aerodrome over land.

SECTION 5 - BOMB THREAT TO AIRCRAFT 
 
5.1 
General 
5.1.1 A bomb threat situation exists when information is received alleging that an 
explosive device has been or will be placed on board an aircraft. 
 
5.1.2 Usually, threats from the public are received by telephone and seldom by written 
message or through personal contacts. In most cases threats are delivered 
anonymously. 
 
5.2 
Threat Classification 
All threats shall be treated as genuine until the Airport Evaluation Committee has 
classified them as NON – SPECIFIC (HOAX) or SPECIFIC (GENUINE). 
 
5.2.1 
Non – Specific (Hoax) 
A threat can be classified as HOAX if it does not consist of any or combination 
of these information: 
a) The identification of the airline. 
b) The flight number. 
c) Date and time. 
d) Point or origin or destination. 
e) Location of the bomb. 
 
 
5.2.2 
Specific Threat (Genuine). 
A threat is classified as Genuine Threat when it consists of any one or a 
combination of the following information: 
a) The originator of the threats identifies himself. 
b) The airline is identified.

e) Location of the bomb. 
 
 
5.2.2 
Specific Threat (Genuine). 
A threat is classified as Genuine Threat when it consists of any one or a 
combination of the following information: 
a) The originator of the threats identifies himself. 
b) The airline is identified. 
c) A specific airline / flight is mentioned. 
d) Exact date and / or time is stated.

availability of aircraft steps, lighting, transport etc to facilitate immediate

SECTION 6 - AIRCRAFT HIJACK 
 
6.1 
Unlawful Seizure 
The “Unlawful Seizure of an aircraft” is an act of air piracy and it’s a violation of 
both Malaysian and International Laws. 
 
6.2 
Airborne Seizure 
a) An aircraft that has been hijacked at some point between take-off and landing 
or has been seized on the ground at another airport either locally or abroad, and 
is airborne at the time it was unlawfully seized. 
 
b) Indication of the occurrence of an unlawful seizure of an aircraft in flight is 
normally transmitted to Air Traffic Controllers by the pilot of the seized aircraft 
by means of coded signal, i.e. Transponder Code of 7500. 
 
6.3 
Designated Aircraft Isolated Area. 
 
 
6.3.1 
It is important that action to be taken to isolate the hijacked aircraft. To permit 
isolation of the aircraft, the airport authority (MAB) shall designate an isolated 
parking position at the aerodrome to which such aircraft may be moved 
immediately. 
 
6.3.2 
The Designated Aircraft Isolated Area should be a minimum of 100 m (328 ft) away 
from any other aircraft parking position, runway, building, public area, fuel tank or 
storage area for explosive or incendiary material. 
 
6.3.3 
Care must be taken to ensure that the Designated Aircraft Isolated Area does not

from any other aircraft parking position, runway, building, public area, fuel tank or 
storage area for explosive or incendiary material. 
 
6.3.3 
Care must be taken to ensure that the Designated Aircraft Isolated Area does not 
have gas pipelines, refuelling hydrants, other fuel lines or electric power cable 
beneath the surface. 
 
Note: At present, taxiway J Runway 15 has been designated as an Isolated Aircraft 
Parking Position for aircraft on hijacks or bomb threat.

6.4 
Actions to be taken by Duty Air Traffic Controller: 
 
 
a) To inform all concerned immediately it is known, observed or suspected that an 
aircraft has been hijacked. Refer Appendix A. 
b) To maintain an ongoing communication link with the seized aircraft. 
c) To maintain all normal flight operations. 
d) To make preparation for landing of the seized aircraft. 
e) To initiate measure to park the seized aircraft in a “Designated Isolated Parking 
Area”. 
f) To preserve all audiotapes and other recorded information after the emergency 
situation is terminated. 
g) A complete ATC report should be submitted to the CAAM Manager for the Chief 
Executive Officer of CAAM. 
h) All actions taken are to be logged down in the logbook.

7.1 
If total radio communication failure occurs to an aircraft bound for the Sultan Abdul 
Aziz Shah Airport, Subang, before entering the Kuala Lumpur FIR or entering the 
FIR but before being given or acknowledging a specific STAR, the pilot-in- 
command shall: 
a) In VMC, during daylight hours, maintain VFR and land at Sultan Abdul Aziz 
Shah Airport, Subang or at a suitable aerodrome. Pilot shall take note that the 
KL International Airport is not to be considered as a suitable aerodrome for this 
purpose 
b) In IMC, or between the hours of sunset and sunrise, proceed via flight plan 
route or as cleared by ATC at last assigned level: 
i) If route terminates at VKL, then from VKL proceed to VBA maintaining the 
last assigned flight level; 
ii) If route terminates at VBA, then proceed to step 7.1, d) 
c) Transmit blind position reports and intentions if the aircraft’s transmitter is 
presumed serviceable; 
d) Commence descent in the VBA hold at, or as close as possible to, the EAT last 
received and acknowledged or, if no EAT has been received and 
acknowledged, at or as close as possible to the EAT calculated from the current 
flight plan; 
e) Carry out an instrument approach procedure for Subang runway 15;

2.1 
GENERAL 
 
2.1.1 From time to time, Police Airwing will need to carry out escort duties leading to 
and out of Sungai Buloh Prison. This requires the aircraft to be within a certain 
distance from the vehicular convoy. Due to the close proximity of Sungai Buloh 
Prison to the approach path of RWY15, these operations affect air movements 
into and out of Subang Airport. 
 
2.1.2 Observations noted from past escort operation show that controllers are often 
placed in a dilemma as there is no specific flight priority to accord such operations.

Prison to the approach path of RWY15, these operations affect air movements 
into and out of Subang Airport. 
 
2.1.2 Observations noted from past escort operation show that controllers are often 
placed in a dilemma as there is no specific flight priority to accord such operations. 
 
2.1.3 To remove this area of ambiguity, Police Airwing aircraft providing escort duties 
over Sungai Buloh Prison will now be accorded priority over aircraft operating a 
scheduled flight but below aircraft engaged in the personal transport of the King, 
PM, DPM or other dignitaries approved by the government.

ACTION 
 
2.2.1 Police Airwing. 
 
a) Provide a minimum 10-minute notification either via VHF or telephone. 
 
b) ETA over Sungai Buloh Prison. 
 
c) Duration over the area. 
 
i) Operate at 300FT and keep a listening watch on 118.2MHz. Once aware

maintained. If unable to maintain visual separation, descend and land at 
open field near the prison. 
 
2.2.2 Subang Tower 
 
a) Suspend “circuit and landing” training flight temporarily. 
 
b) Issue missed approach instructions early, preferably at downwind, to the IFR 
arrival making a visual approach for RWY33.

circumstances shall be similar to military flights. MMEA flights are sometimes 
specifically tasked to do maritime search and rescue. They may also be enlisted

2.4 
Wind Indicator and Runway Visual Range (WRVR) 
 
2.4.1 Introduction 
 
WRVR is an automated system providing accurate wind and runway visual range 
data by using intelligent sensor to Selangor Meteorology office and Subang Tower. 
It consists of a set of wind and visibility sensor and installed at the end of runway. 
The weather data captured by the sensors will be transmitted through wireless 
network to the Selangor Meteorology office for data processing. The derived 
information will then be made accessible to Subang Tower via internet through a 
web browser. All the data generated will be transmitted to National Aeronautical 
Meteorology Centre (NAMC). 
 
2.4.2 Accessing Wind Indicator and Runway Visual Range (WRVR)

2.4.3.1 Runway Visual Range (RVR) 
 
a) In the event of Automated RVR failure, RVR can be obtain manually by Human 
Observer Technique as per method below: 
 
i. 
This method involves counting the number of runway edge lights that can be 
seen by an observer from the touchdown zone of a runway.

ii. 
The number of lights observed is converted into a RVR range using the 
distance between each light and, after making due allowance for differences in 
light intensity, background, etc. For simplicity however, a straight conversion is 
usually done. 
 
iii. 
The observation should preferably be taken standing on a suitable vehicle to 
simulate as far as practicable the cockpit height – usually 5 metres with the 
runway lights normally set at maximum intensity. 
 
b) Controller shall request MASB operator (Ops 1) to perform Human Observation

General Administration  
2.1 
Introduction 
 
Aircraft operations in Malaysia are regulated in accordance with the Civil Aviation 
Act (CAA) 1969 and Civil Aviation Regulations (CAR) 2016. The Chief Executive 
Officer (CEO) of Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) assumes overall 
responsibility for promoting the safety and efficiency of civil aviation in Malaysia in 
accordance with the CAA 1969, CAR 2016, CADs, Civil Aviation Guidance 
Materials, CAAM Act 2017 and Civil Aviation (Amendment) Regulations 2018. He 
advises the Government on all policy matters concerning international civil aviation 
including those pertaining to the provision of air traffic services. As a contracting 
state to International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), air traffic services within 
the airspace under the control of Malaysia are provided in conformity with the

In an ATC operational environment, the handover and takeover watch process is 
a standard but safety-critical task that needs to be completed thoroughly and 
accurately. It is to ensure that the incoming (takeover) controller will acquire an 
adequate overview not only of the traffic situation but also of the control strategies 
of the outgoing (handover) controller.

Handover-Takeover Basic Principles 
 
ATCs shall adopt four basics principles during HOW-TOW: 
 Handover commences in a “clean” situation, (i.e., there is no emergency 
or abnormal situation developing and the conflicts are either solved or a 
plan to resolve has been made); 
 The takeover (incoming) controller shall arrive earlier and the handover 
(outgoing) controller shall remain near the working position until he/she is 
certain that the situational awareness of the incoming controller is at a 
desired level; 
 
A HOW-TOW Quick Reference in the form of a checklist shall be used as 
a guideline so that any vital information is not neglected or omitted; and 
 Both controllers shall sign the HOW-TOW Quick Reference to 
acknowledge all information given/relay by the handover controller. 
 
The Handover/Takeover Watch shall: 
 Be conducted at a distance that both controllers should be able to listen 
attentively to each other;  
 Be in a two-way, with both controllers taking joint responsibility to ensure 
the exchange of accurate information and effective communication takes 
place; 
 
Use verbal and written means of communication; 
 Be accommodated as much time as necessary to complete the process; 
and 
 Be conducted by rated working controllers and not by a trainee or someone 
else, except for training purposes.

The ILS inspection may take between 1.5 to 2 hours to assess the localizer 
(LOC) course alignment, glide path (GP) angular alignment, marker operation 
and alarm settings.  
 
The flight inspection aircraft shall execute nine different profiles, in order to 
complete the ILS inspection, and some profiles may be repeated. The 
descriptions of each profile are stated below: 
 Profile 01 - Centreline (Descending Run Down to 50 ft) 
1) The purpose is to check the LOC course, GP slope and alarms.

runway centreline, at a distance and height to be coordinated with

whether the facility is CAT I or CAT II. 
4) As soon as the 50 ft AGL point is reached, the pilot of the flight 
inspection aircraft will overshoot the runway, and indicate to ATC a left 
or right turn to position for next inspection profile.

VOR/TACAN Inspection 
 
VOR/TACAN inspection will involve two 360° anti-clockwise orbits around the 
facility at a constant height to check the two transmitters.  
 
For periodic inspection, a 10 NM orbit centred on the VOR/TACAN will be 
undertaken and while orbiting a few reference radials associated with the 
runway headings and/or ATS routes will be inspected. 
 
For commissioning inspection, the following procedures will be undertaken: 
 360° anti-clockwise orbits, one each at 20 NM and 40 NM centred on the 
facility; and  
 Flight inspection of at least eight radials. Additional radials, normally 
associated with selected ATS routes or instrument procedures, may be 
flown if so required by the CEO. 
 
The flight inspection aircraft will fly the orbit at a minimum safe altitude, that is, 
the height of the highest terrain or obstruction within the orbit sector plus 1,000 
ft. When radials are flown for commissioning inspection, the height flown will be 
dependent on the terrain within a sector. The pilot of the flight inspection aircraft 
shall notify ATC of the altitude to be flown.

airborne systems capable of guiding the aircraft with greater accuracy to the

Controller Working Positions Combined Procedure  
 
Recognising the importance of operational efficiency and safety in the dynamic 
field of air traffic services, there is a need of combining controller working positions 
depending on traffic volume and complexity of the control area to meet varying 
operational demands.  
 
This procedure is intended to serve as a guideline for combining controller working 
positions with the optimal use of manpower and resources.  
 
The purposes of this procedure are to: 
 Define the factors to be considered when combining controller working 
positions; and 
 Describe the procedures on combining controller working positions. 
 
Factors to be considered for combining controller working positions without 
compromising safety includes, but not limited to:   
 The Area of Responsibility (AOR) continues to have reliable radio frequency 
coverage after the combination; 
 Combination of the Controller Working Position (CWP) is feasible;  
 
Configuration of controller working positions depending on the traffic volume 
and anticipated workload;   
 Station’s staff strength is not capable of fulfilling the manpower required to 
operate in normal working positions; or  
 During the activation of Business Continuity Plan (BCP).  
 
The process of combining working positions needs to be carefully refined to ensure

 Station’s staff strength is not capable of fulfilling the manpower required to 
operate in normal working positions; or  
 During the activation of Business Continuity Plan (BCP).

operational smoothness without compromising safety and the quality of air

Introduction 
 
This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective. 
Throughout this MATS Volume 1, the use of masculine pronouns should be understood to 
represent male and female persons.

1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 10 - Coordination, Issue 
02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 10 - Coordination shall be read together 
with Civil Aviation Regulation 2016, International Civil Aviation Organization Doc 
4444, Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 1, CAD 2, CAD 11, CAD 12, CAD 1007 and 
CAD 1101. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 10 - Coordination contains standard operating 
procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other operational 
personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their area of 
responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026. 
1.4

Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788]. 
May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative. 
Miles always refers to nautical miles (NM). 
Shall, is to, are to and must means the instruction is mandatory.  
Should means that the procedure or instruction is recommended. It is applied where

 Coordination Environments  
 
Air Traffic Control (ATC) procedures vary significantly, depending on the 
surveillance capabilities of the coordinating ATSUs in a given boundary 
environment. For the purpose of this subchapter the coordination environments 
are identified as either surveillance or procedural. In some instances, the same 
type of message may require the inclusion of different or additional data to 
accommodate the demands of differing environments. Depending on the
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 10 - COORDINATION (03072026).pdf

text:
are identified as either surveillance or procedural. In some instances, the same 
type of message may require the inclusion of different or additional data to 
accommodate the demands of differing environments. Depending on the 
environment, the timing of the transmission of these messages may also vary. 
The environment may also affect whether the AIDC message is automatically 
processed, or displayed to the controller for manual processing.  
 
A surveillance environment is an environment where an ATS surveillance 
system is in use, and allows controllers to positively identify the traffic. Radar 
and/or Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast (ADS-B) are available to 
the controllers at sector positions on both sides of a common boundary, and 
traffic is identified by information presented on a situation display. Such facilities 
permit surveillance coordination procedures to be used.  
 
 A procedural environment exists in those areas where surveillance 
coordination procedures are not available because at least one of the 
coordinating ATSUs does not have a surveillance capability, or the surveillance 
capabilities differ. For example, surveillance in oceanic and remote areas is 
often achieved with Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Contract (ADS-C), 
Controller Pilot Data Link Communications (CPDLC) or voice position reports; 
in such areas, coordination procedures differ from those used in a surveillance 
environment.

Runway Visual range (RVR) is defined as the range over which the pilot of an 
aircraft on the centreline of a runway can see the runway surface markings or 
the lights delineating the runway or identifying its centreline. RVR is not a 
“measurement” or “observation” of a meteorological parameter such as wind 
direction and speed, temperature or pressure. It is an assessment that takes 
into account a number of factors both atmospheric and non-atmospheric.

minima. More generally, pilots use the RVR as an indication of the visual

Search and Rescue Requirements 
 
RCCs shall maintain close liaison with the MET office to obtain the required 
information for SAR operations. Information required by the RCCs shall include, if 
possible, the meteorological conditions that existed in the last known position of 
the missing aircraft and along the intended route of the aircraft with particular 
reference to: 
 Significant en route weather phenomena; 
 Cloud amount and type, specifically cumulonimbus, and height indications of 
bases and tops; 
 
Visibility and phenomena reducing visibility; 
 Surface wind and upper wind; 
 State of ground, in particular, any flooding; 
 
Surface sea temperature, state of the sea, ocean currents if relevant; and 
 Sea level pressure data. 
 
The RCC shall arrange with the MET office for the following: 
 Meteorological information that were supplied to the missing aircraft, e.g., 
route forecasts; 
 Complete and detailed information on the current, 48-hour history and 
forecast meteorological conditions in the search area(s); 
 
Current and forecast conditions en route and at aerodromes, as appropriate, 
for search aircraft.

latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and

context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller.

General 
 
The lead-time requirements of air traffic control and flow control procedures shall 
determine the method of message exchange to be used for the exchange of ATS 
data. 
 
The method of message exchange shall also be dependent upon the availability 
of adequate communications channels, the function to be performed, the types of 
data to be exchanged and the processing facilities at the centres concerned. 
 
Basic flight plan data necessary for flow control procedures shall be furnished at 
least 60 minutes in advance of the flight. Basic flight plan data shall be provided 
by either a filed flight plan or a repetitive flight plan submitted by mail in the form 
of a repetitive flight plan listing form or other media suitable for electronic data-
processing systems.

route changes and other essential information as may be necessary.

to the first en route control centre at least 30 minutes in advance of the flight, and 
to each successive centre at least 20 minutes before the aircraft enters that 
centre’s area of jurisdiction, in order for it to prepare for the transfer of control.

Data Conventions 
 
Most of the conventions to be used in the expression of ATS data in the 
messages are prescribed in the field tables on pages A3-6 to A3-34 ICAO Doc 
4444 but the conventions for the expression of level, position and route data 
are given below to simplify the field tables. 
 
The Expression of Level Data 
6.1.7.2.1 
Four alternative conventions are available for the expression of level data: 
a) “F” followed by 3 decimal numerics: indicates a flight level number, i.e., 
Flight Level 330 is expressed as “F330”; 
b) “S” followed by 4 decimal numerics: indicates standard metric level in 
tens of metres, i.e., Standard Metric Level 11 300 metres (Flight Level 
370) is expressed as “S1130”; 
c) “A” followed by 3 decimal numerics: indicates altitude in hundreds of feet, 
i.e., an altitude of 4 500 feet is expressed as “A045”;

c) “A” followed by 3 decimal numerics: indicates altitude in hundreds of feet,

d) “M” followed by 4 decimal numerics: indicates altitude in tens of metres,

6.1.7.3.1 
The following alternative data conventions shall be used for the expression

describing longitude in degrees and tens and units of minutes, followed

made up, where necessary, by the insertion of zeros, e.g., 
“4620N07805W”;

(See Sections 1.3 to 1.8 of this Appendix)
 
Composition of the standard types of message 
 
The composition of each standard type of 
message, expressed as a standardized sequence of 
fields of data, shall be as prescribed in the reference 
table on this page. Each message shall contain all the 
fields prescribed. 
 
Composition of the standard types of field 
 
The composition of each standard type of field, 
expressed as a standardised sequence of elements of 
data, or in some cases as a simple element, shall be as 
prescribed in the field tables on pages A3-6 to AP-C-
26. 
 
Note: Each type of field contains at least one 
mandatory element and, except in Field Type 9, this is 
the first or only element in the field. The rules for the 
inclusion or omission of conditional elements are 
indicated in the field tables.

Data conventions 
 
    
Most of the conventions to be used in the 
expression of ATS data in the messages are prescribed 
in the field tables on pages AP-C-5 to AP-C-26, but 
the conventions for the expression of level, position 
and route data are given below. 
 
The expression of level data 
 
Four alternative conventions are available for the 
expression of level data: 
 
(a) “F” followed by 3 decimal numerics: 
 
indicates a flight level number, i.e. Flight Level

Four alternative conventions are available for the 
expression of level data: 
 
(a) “F” followed by 3 decimal numerics: 
 
indicates a flight level number, i.e. Flight Level 
340 is expressed as “F340”; 
 
(b) “S” followed by 4 decimal numerics: 
indicates standard metric level in tens of metres, 
i.e. Standard Metric Level 11 300 m (Flight Level 
370) is expressed as “S1130”; 
 
(c)  “A” followed by 3 decimal numerics: 
indicates altitude in hundreds of feet, i.e. an 
altitude of 4,500 ft is expressed as “A045”; 
 
(d) “M” followed by 4 decimal numerics: 
indicates altitude in tens of metres, i.e. an altitude 
of 8,400 m is expressed as “M0840”. 
 
The expression of position or route 
 
The following alternative data conventions shall be 
used for the expression of position or route: 
 
(a) from 2 to 7 characters, being the coded 
designator assigned to an ATS route to be flown; 
 
 
b)  from 2 to 5 characters, being the coded designator 
 
assigned to an en route point; 
 
(c)  4 numerics describing latitude in degrees and tens 
 
and units of minutes, followed by “N” (meaning 
 
“North”) or “S” (South), followed by 5 numerics 
 
describing longitude in degrees and tens and units 
 
of minutes, followed by “E” (East) or “W” 
(West). The correct number of numerics is to be 
made up, where necessary, by the insertion of 
zeros, e.g “4620N07805W”; 
 
(d)  2 numerics describing latitude in degrees, 
followed by “N” (North) or “S” (South), followed
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 11 - AIR TRAFFIC SERVICES MESSAGES (03072026).pdf

text:
of minutes, followed by “E” (East) or “W” 
(West). The correct number of numerics is to be 
made up, where necessary, by the insertion of 
zeros, e.g “4620N07805W”; 
 
(d)  2 numerics describing latitude in degrees, 
followed by “N” (North) or “S” (South), followed 
by 3 numerics describing longitude in degrees, 
followed by “E” (East) or “W” (West). Again, the 
correct number of numerics is to be made up, 
where necessary, by the insertion of zeros, e.g. 
“46N078W”; 
 
(e)  2 to 5 characters being the coded identification of 
a significant point, followed by 3 decimal 
numerics giving the bearing from the point in 
degrees magnetic followed by 3 decimal numerics 
giving the distance from the point in nautical 
miles. In areas of high latitude where it is 
determined by the appropriate authority that 
reference to degrees magnetic is impractical, 
degrees true may be used. The correct number of 
numerics is to be made up, where necessary, by 
the insertion of zeros, e.g. a point at 180° 
magnetic at a distance of 40 NM from VOR 
“VAS” would be expressed as “VAS180040”.

The elements of data prescribed or permitted to be 
included in each type of field, together with a 
prescription of the conditions or options permitted, are 
shown on pages AP-C-5 to AP-C-26. 
 
A key appears at the right-hand side of each of the 
field pages; this key permits the sequence of fields in 
each type of message to be followed.

Composition - (Field Types 3, 7 and 21)

related ATSUs informing them of a radio communication failure on a flight. The 
related flight plan shows that the aircraft is not equipped with a SSR 
transponder. 
(RCF - THA402

 THA402) 
 
Meaning 
Radio communication failure message - aircraft identification is THA402 - last 
communication with Lumpur Radio was at position 0600N 09440E at 0925UTC 
on 11285kHz. The remaining communication capabilities of the aircraft are VHF 
and UHF - information on the HF failure of the aircraft was relayed by MAC 
50253 who will stand guard and relay future position of the aircraft.

Introduction 
 
This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective. 
Throughout this MATS Volume 1, the use of masculine pronouns should be understood to 
represent male and female persons.
