Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 12 - Phraseologies, 
Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 12 - Phraseologies shall be read 
together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 11, CAD 1101, International Civil 
Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 9683, ICAO Doc 9869 and ICAO Doc 10037. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 12 - Phraseologies contains standard operating 
procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other operational 
personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their area of 
responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3

This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026.

2 
General Provisions 
2.1 
Introduction 
 
Precise and unambiguous communications between controllers and pilots and, 
between controllers themselves is extremely important in air traffic service to meet 
the objectives of safety and efficiency. This is all the more important because of 
the diverse nationalities and languages involved. Accordingly, ICAO has 
developed a comprehensive list of phrases, which are designed to be precise and 
concise, for use in air traffic services. 
 
This part lays down the procedures, phraseology and guidance material with the 
objective of ensuring uniformity in telephone and Radio Telephony (RTF) 
communications. 
 
Controllers and other Air Traffic Services (ATS) personnel shall observe the 
highest standard of discipline at all times with respect to the use of the standard 
phraseology given in the MATS. Controllers may, on occasions find it necessary 
to extend or modify the phraseology but in doing so they should take care not to 
deviate from or prejudice basic meanings or intentions. 
 
They are not intended to be exhaustive, and when circumstances differ, pilots, 
ATS personnel and other ground personnel will be expected to use plain language, 
which should be as clear and concise as possible, to the level specified in the 
ICAO language proficiency requirements contained in CAD 1007 - English
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 12 - PHRASEOLOGIES (03072026).pdf

text:
ATS personnel and other ground personnel will be expected to use plain language, 
which should be as clear and concise as possible, to the level specified in the 
ICAO language proficiency requirements contained in CAD 1007 - English 
Language Proficiency Testing (ELPT). 
 
Controllers should avoid: 
 too rapid delivery of instructions especially with pilots who are not fluent in the 
English language; 
 the assumption that visiting pilots are as familiar with the local area and airfield 
as the locally based pilots; 
 
verbosity and excessive use of courtesies; 
 using hesitation syllables such as “er” or “ah” “mmm” etc.; and 
 entering into non-operational conversation with pilots. 
 
Controllers shall not direct transmission to an aircraft during take-off, during the 
last part of the final approach or during the landing roll except for reasons of safety. 
 
During busy periods when simultaneous calls from several aircraft are likely, 
controllers should decide on the order of reply based on the disposition of the 
traffic at that time.

2.2 
Speech Technique 
 
The correct enunciation of words, spoken at a uniform rate, will do much to assist 
the satisfactory reception of speech through the telephone and radio media 
including HF. In this connection controllers should: 
 speak directly into the microphones or telephone mouthpieces as these have 
highly directional properties; 
 avoid “clipping” transmissions, particularly when the transmitter is remote from 
the ATS Unit; and 
 
depress the transmit switch fully before speech is commenced and to release 
the switch only after the transmission is completed. 
 
Controllers shall first identify themselves in relation to their operating position 
when answering a call on the intercom, telephone system or radio. This will confirm 
to the caller that he is communicating with the right person at the other end. 
Example:  
 “Lumpur Sector 2” if responding to say Singapore on the direct line; 
 “Sector 2” if responding to another work position within the same unit on the 
intercom; 
 
“…(callsign)…This is Lumpur Radar” when first responding to an aircraft on 
RTF. 
 
Controllers shall take note that communications equipment have automatic gain 
control circuit design built-in, which will automatically adjust signal levels. This 
permits speech at normal conversational levels. 
2.3

Controllers shall take note that communications equipment have automatic gain 
control circuit design built-in, which will automatically adjust signal levels. This 
permits speech at normal conversational levels. 
2.3 
RTF and Intercom Procedures and Techniques 
 
RTF always has priority over intercom or telephones. 
 
When an aircraft calls, the controllers must listen carefully, record and check the 
details of the message and acknowledge immediately. If a pilot requests 
information or a clearance which is not immediately available, the controller must 
acknowledge and advise the pilot to “standby” whilst the required information or 
clearance is obtained. The pilot’s call must not be ignored whilst the information/ 
clearance is being obtained as this will cause the pilot to repeat his requests. 
 
If a controller is coordinating on the intercom when an aircraft calls, he must 
immediately give attention to the pilot’s message and acknowledge before 
proceeding with the intercom call. In such instances, it will be appropriate to say 
“standby” or “call you back” to the person on the intercom. 
 
When replying to aircraft transmissions, controllers shall acknowledge by using 
the aircraft callsign, and NOT by using “Roger”.

Chapter 2 - General Provisions 
 
 
 
2-3
 
Controllers must not acknowledge messages that are not received or copied in full 
or not fully understood. This applies to both RTF and intercom. The pilot or other 
party should be asked to “say again” or “confirm” the message or items which are 
not clear. 
 
Controller must not accept incomplete messages or inadequate information. It is 
their responsibility to insist on obtaining the complete details. 
 
To ensure the efficiency of communications, controllers shall prefix their message 
during routine coordination so that the person being called will immediately 
recognise the type of message that he/she is to expect. The following prefixes 
shall be used in routine coordination: 
DEP, EST, Approval Request, Revision, Clearance, Sequence, Inbound Release 
and EAT. 
 
When calling on a “hot line” facility, controllers shall first listen to ensure that the 
controller being called is not engaged on the R/T or on the intercom before passing 
the message to the controller.

4.1 
Aircraft Callsigns 
 
An aircraft radiotelephony call sign shall be one of the following types: 
 Type a) - the characters corresponding to the registration marking of the 
aircraft; or  
 Type b) - the telephony designator of the aircraft operating agency, followed 
by the last four characters of the registration marking of the aircraft;  
 
Type c) - the telephony designator of the aircraft operating agency, followed 
by the flight identification.  
Note. - The name of the aircraft manufacturer or of the aircraft model may be used 
as a radiotelephony prefix to the Type a) call sign (see Table 4-1).

controllers are permitted to abbreviate the callsign but only to the extent shown in

characters of the call sign;

by at least the last two characters of the call sign;

Callsign Confusion 
 
The similarity of some aircraft callsigns on the same frequency can cause

Telephone Arrangements 
5.1 
General 
 
While most ATS Units are equipped with Subscriber Trunk Dialling (STD) 
telephones, there may be instances to obtain the services of the telephone 
network provider to connect calls. Three priority categories of call are available to 
ATC and their order of priority are: 
 Distress Call; 
 Lightning Call; 
 
Urgent Call. 
 
The prefix “Distress Call” is reserved for extreme operationally urgent situations or 
when immediate connection is essential because safety of human life is involved. 
“Distress Calls” have absolute priority over all other calls and will be connected 
immediately, other calls being disconnected if necessary. 
 
The prefix “Lightning Call” is strictly reserved for calls relating to operational 
matters which may develop into “Distress” and for most urgent matters of essential 
administrative importance. A “Lightning Call” will be connected ahead of “Urgent” 
and other calls which have been booked. Existing calls will not be disconnected 
for “Lightning Calls” but such calls will be offered to engaged extensions. 
 
The prefix “Urgent Call” is reserved for calls of urgent operational or administrative 
importance. An “Urgent Call” takes precedence over all except “Distress” and 
“Lightning” calls. Existing calls will not be disconnected for “Urgent Calls” such 
calls will be offered to engaged extensions.

latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and

General 
1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 15 - Procedures 
Related to Emergencies, Communication Failure and Contingencies, Issue 
02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 15 - Procedures Related to 
Emergencies, Communication Failure and Contingencies shall be read together 
with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 2, CAD 10 Volume II, CAD 11, CAD 1101, CAD 
12, CAD 14, International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 7030, ICAO Doc 
8168, ICAO Doc 9691, ICAO Doc 9863 and ICAO Doc 10037. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
This manual contains standard operating procedures, act as guidance material for 
air traffic controllers and other operational personnel tasked with the provision of 
air traffic services under their area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026. 
1.4 
Interpretation of Words 
Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788]. 
May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative. 
Miles always refers to nautical miles (NM).

Chapter 2 - Emergency Procedures 
 
 
 
2-1
2 
Emergency Procedures 
2.1 
General 
 
The various circumstances surrounding each emergency situation preclude the 
establishment of exact detailed procedures to be followed. The procedures 
outlined herein are intended as a general guide to air traffic services personnel. 
Air traffic control units shall maintain full and complete coordination, and personnel 
shall use their best judgement in handling emergency situations. 
Note1. - Additional procedures to be applied in relation to emergencies and 
contingencies while using an Air Traffic Services (ATS) surveillance system are 
contained in Part 8, Chapter 9. 
Note2. - If the pilot of an aircraft encountering a state of emergency has previously 
been directed by Air Traffic Control (ATC) to select a specific transponder code 
and/or a specific Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast (ADS-B) 
emergency mode, that code and/or mode will normally be maintained unless, in 
special circumstances, the pilot has decided or has been advised otherwise. 
Where ATC has not requested a code or emergency mode to be set, the pilot will 
set the transponder to Mode A Code 7700 and/or the appropriate ADS-B 
emergency mode. 
Note3. - Some aircraft equipped with first generation ADS-B avionics have the 
capability to transmit a general emergency alert only, regardless of the code 
selected by the pilot.

Note4. - Some aircraft equipped with first generation ADS-B avionics do not have

When an emergency is declared by an aircraft, the Air Traffic Services Unit (ATSU) 
shall take appropriate and relevant action as follows: 
 Unless clearly stated by the flight crew or otherwise known, take all necessary 
steps to ascertain aircraft identification and type, the type of emergency, the 
intentions of the flight crew as well as the position and level of the aircraft; 
 Decide upon the most appropriate type of assistance which can be rendered; 
 
Enlist the aid of any other ATSU or other services which may be able to 
provide assistance to the aircraft; 
 Provide the flight crew with any information requested as well as any 
additional relevant information, such as details on suitable aerodromes, 
minimum safe altitudes, weather information; 
 Obtain from the operator or the flight crew such of the following information 
as may be relevant: number of persons on board, amount of fuel remaining, 
possible presence of hazardous materials and the nature thereof; and

Chapter 2 - Emergency Procedures 
 
 
 
2-2
 
Changes of radio frequency and Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR) code shall 
be avoided if possible and shall normally be made only when or if an improved 
service can be provided to the aircraft concerned. Manoeuvring instructions to an 
aircraft experiencing engine failure shall be limited to a minimum. When 
appropriate, other aircraft operating in the vicinity of the aircraft in emergency shall 
be advised of the circumstances. 
Note. - Requests to the flight crew for the information contained in paragraph 2.1.2 
e) will be made only if the information is not available from the operator or from 
other sources and will be limited to essential information. 
2.2 
Guidelines 
 
Controllers shall apply the rules and procedures in this section as the basis for 
handling aircraft emergencies. Different circumstances may affect an emergency 
and because of this it is not possible to specify procedures to cover every 
emergency situation. Controllers are therefore expected to use their best 
judgement to assess and handle a situation not specifically covered in this manual. 
 
If circumstances dictate, controllers may vary the standard radiotelephony 
phraseology and procedures to handle an emergency situation. However, 
controllers shall always bear in mind the need to be precise and, to take into 
consideration aircrew workload during emergencies.

Emergency Separation 
 
If, during an emergency situation, it is not possible to ensure that the applicable 
horizontal separation can be maintained, emergency separation of half the 
applicable vertical separation minimum may be used, i.e., 500 ft (150 m) between 
aircraft in airspace where a vertical separation minimum of 1,000 ft (300 m) is 
applied, and 300 m (1,000 ft) between aircraft in airspace where a 2,000 ft (600 
m) vertical separation minimum is applied.

advised that emergency separation is being applied and informed of the actual 
minimum used. Additionally, all flight crews concerned shall be provided with 
essential traffic information.

The ICAO established the Global Aeronautical Distress and Safety System

the timely identification and localisation of aircraft in distress, including lessons 
learned from accidents such as Air France flight AF447 and Malaysia Airlines

GADSS provides a globally consistent approach to enhancing the alerting 
procedures of SAR services, comprises three (3) main elements:  
 
Aircraft tracking; 
 
Location of an aircraft in distress through Autonomous Distress Tracking 
(ADT); and 
 
Post-flight localisation and recovery (PFLR). 
 
Through these elements, GADSS enhances the availability of aircraft position

Reported or Forecast 
9.1 
ATC Action 
 
If a volcanic ash cloud is reported or forecast in the airspace for which the ATSU 
is responsible, the following actions shall be taken: 
 Relay pertinent information immediately to flight crews whose aircraft could 
be affected to ensure that they are aware of the ash cloud’s current and 
forecast position and the flight levels affected; 
 Accommodate requests for re-routing or level changes to the extent 
practicable; 
 
Suggest re-routing to avoid or exit areas of reported or forecast ash clouds 
when requested by the pilot or deemed necessary by the controller; and 
 When practicable, request a special air-report when the route of flight takes 
the aircraft into or near the forecast ash cloud and provide such special air-
reports to the appropriate agencies. 
Note1. - Experience has shown that the recommended escape manoeuvre for an 
aircraft which has encountered an ash cloud is to reverse its course and begin a 
descent if terrain permits. The final responsibility for this decision, however, rests 
with the pilot-in-command as specified in the Manual on Volcanic Ash, Radioactive 
Material and Toxic Chemical Clouds (ICAO Doc 9691), Paragraph 5.2.4.1.

Wind Shear Hazards at Aerodromes 
10.1 
General 
 
Wind shear is a sustained change in wind velocity along an aircraft’s flight path, 
which occurs significantly faster than the aircraft can accelerate or decelerate. 
Wind shear can occur at any level, but it is the “low level wind shear” occurring 
from the surface to a height of approximately 1,500 ft, which causes problems of 
sufficient magnitude to affect the control of aircraft in the departure and approach 
phases of flight. 
 
At aerodromes, controllers shall be alert to the following conditions which are 
conducive to wind shear: 
 The presence of a front, squall or thunderstorm activity in the vicinity of the 
aerodrome; and 
 The presence of low-level inversion where the surface wind will be 
significantly different from that at only a few hundred feet above the ground. 
 
Controllers shall also be aware that obstructions within an aerodrome such as 
local terrain or buildings considered in relation to wind speed and direction, can 
cause wind shear in addition to the usual generation of turbulence and gusts.

Note1. - Strategic Lateral Offset Procedures (SLOP) are approved procedures that allow 
aircraft to fly on a parallel track to the right of the centre line relative to the direction of flight to

turbulence encounters. Unless specified in the separation standard, an aircraft’s use of these 
procedures does not affect the application of prescribed separation standards.

lateral offsets from the appropriate ATS authority responsible for the airspace concerned.

Introduction 
 
To ensure the safe and successful implementation of Reduced Vertical Separation 
Minimum (RVSM) operation, there are two risk components that must be 
monitored, they are; 
 Technical risk relates to the technical performance of equipment, including 
altimetry systems; and 
 Operational risk relates to human performance error and, in simple terms, 
considers errors made by pilots and air traffic controllers. 
 
MAAR was established by AEROTHAI aiming to furthering the implementation of 
RVSM in the Asia region. 
 
MAAR officially assumed the duties and responsibilities of the Regional Monitoring 
Agency (RMA) for the Asia region on September 2, 2003. 
 
The principal duties and responsibilities of MAAR consist of the followings:  
 Establish and maintain a database of RVSM approvals;  
 Monitor aircraft height-keeping performance and the occurrence of LHDs and 
report the results appropriately;  
 
Conduct safety and readiness assessments and report the results 
appropriately;  
 Monitor operator compliance with State approval requirements; and

Large Height Deviation (LHD)  
 
In general, LHD means a vertical deviation of 300 FT or more from controller 
assigned or coordinated flight level, for any reason, regardless whether the 
deviation causes an incident or not.   
 
The deviation may be due to controller error, pilot error, equipment malfunction or 
other environmental factors such as turbulence, causing the aircraft to be at a 
vertical position that is unexpected by the controller.   
 
The causal errors and examples of LHD are classified in the following taxonomy, 
whereby any LHD reports to MAAR should be in accordance with the listed codes.  
 
Code  
LHD Cause  
Operational Errors  
A  
Flight crew failing to climb/descend the aircraft as cleared  
 
Example: Aircraft A was at FL300 and assigned FL360. A Cleared Level Adherence 
Monitoring (CLAM) alert was seen as the aircraft passed FL364. The Mode C level 
reached FL365 before descending back to FL360.  
 
B  
Flight crew climbing/descending without air traffic control (ATC) clearance

INMARSAT, in conjunction with ICAO, has developed a telephone numbering

backup to the existing primary A/G facilities. The use of SATCOM voice for this 
purpose requires on board embedded equipment. 
 
Flight Crew Procedures 
 
The number of call attempts made to establish contact with the radio station will 
be a pilot responsibility; however, if contact cannot be established within 5 
minutes of waypoint transition, pilots should revert to the assigned HF 
frequencies for position report delivery. 
 
On initial contact with a radio station, the flight crew should provide aircraft 
identification and request frequency assignment and perform a successful 
SELCAL check on HF, when required by the CEO. Subsequent 
communications with that radio station may then be performed via SATCOM or 
HF voice, in accordance with applicable airworthiness, operating and airspace 
requirements. 
 
Although the underlying technology lends itself to a conversational mode of 
communications, such use can create misunderstanding and confusion. When 
using SATCOM, normal RTF conventions should be followed identical to HF 
communications in accordance with standard ICAO phraseology, as defined in
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 16 - MISCELLANEOUS PROCEDURES (03072026).pdf

Although the underlying technology lends itself to a conversational mode of

using SATCOM, normal RTF conventions should be followed identical to HF 
communications in accordance with standard ICAO phraseology, as defined in 
Jeppesen ATC- Air Traffic Management (ICAO Doc 4444) \ Section 12, or in 
Annex 10, Volume II, Chapter 5 and ICAO Doc 8400. 
 
The flight crew should normally make calls to the radio facility serving the 
airspace in which the aircraft is flying. If oceanic airspace has not been entered, 
the flight crew should attempt contact with the radio facility serving the first 
oceanic centre. If a call is dropped during a communication, the party that 
initiated the original call should initiate the process to re-establish the call. If 
communications are lost with the current aeronautical station, the flight crew 
should attempt contact with any other aeronautical station to relay. 
 
If a HF SELCAL check is required before or after entering a FIR, the flight crew 
should contact the radio operator and complete a HF SELCAL check in 
accordance with ICAO Annex 10, Volume II, paragraph 5.2.4.

Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and

the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

Airspace Management 
2.1 
Introduction 
 
By international agreement, Malaysia is responsible for the management of the 
airspace and provision of Air Traffic Services (ATS) within the Kuala Lumpur and 
Kota Kinabalu Flight Information Regions (FIRs) and in the South China Sea 
Corridor. Through bilateral agreements, the Air Traffic Services Centres at Kuala 
Lumpur and Kota Kinabalu provide ATS in certain airspace delegated by ATS 
authorities of adjacent FIRs. 
 
The Civil Aviation Regulations 2016 and the relevant ICAO Annexes empower the 
Minister of Transport and the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of CAAM to regulate 
the conduct of air navigation in the two FIRs. Thus, the organisation of airspace 
and provision of air traffic services is in compliance with ICAO. 
 
Airspace activities within the FIRs are not only confined to commercial, private and 
military aviation activities but also include air and surface firing, military training, 
parachute jumping and other activities. 
 
Portions of the airspace in the FIRs have been delineated specifically for safety 
and national security reasons, e.g., to facilitate the provision of air traffic services 
and the conduct of military operations. Some of the activities are incompatible and, 
therefore, require segregation from each other. Certain portions of the airspace
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 17 - AIRSPACE MANAGEMENT (03072026).pdf

text:
and national security reasons, e.g., to facilitate the provision of air traffic services 
and the conduct of military operations. Some of the activities are incompatible and, 
therefore, require segregation from each other. Certain portions of the airspace 
have been delegated to the military, and responsibility for the provision of air traffic 
services in this airspace has been vested with the military. 
 
While the CAAM, the administrative authority, has national responsibility for the 
management of the airspace and the provision of air traffic services in the FIRs, it 
does so on a cooperative basis with the military, which has responsibility for 
national airspace security. 
2.2 
Airspace Administration 
 
Though the primary users of the airspace are civil aircraft operators and the 
military, no single party can claim exclusivity to its use. In planning the organisation 
of the airspace, the principle that shall be adhered to is that airspace organisation 
must provide for an equitable sharing of its use by all those having a legitimate 
interest in it. The objective should be to organise the airspace so that the parties 
concerned can use it most flexibly through a coordinated effort. Furthermore, 
because of the international character of civil aviation, airspace planning of 
necessity should consider regional needs.

Chapter 3 - Airspace Classification 
 
 
 
 
3-1
3 
Airspace Classification 
3.1 
General 
 
The airspace in the two FIRs is classified in accordance with the ICAO 
classification of airspace with the exception that two-way radio communication is 
required of Visual Flight Rules (VFR) aircraft in all classes of airspace. Whenever 
a controlled area is designated, it shall be designated in accordance with this 
classification.  
 
The ATS airspace classifications are as follows: 
Class A 
Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) flights only are permitted. All flights 
are subject to air traffic control service and are separated from 
each other. 
Class B 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All flights are subject to air 
traffic control service and are separated from each other. 
Class C 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All flights are subject to air 
traffic control service and IFR flights are separated from other 
IFR flights and from VFR flights. VFR flights are separated from 
IFR flights and receive traffic information in respect of other VFR 
flights. 
Class D 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All flights are subject to air 
traffic control service. IFR flights are separated from other IFR 
flights and receive traffic information in respect of VFR flights. 
VFR flights receive traffic information in respect of all other 
flights. 
Class E 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. IFR flights are provided with
source: MATS VOLUME 1 ISS.02 REV.02 PART 17 - AIRSPACE MANAGEMENT (03072026).pdf

text:
traffic control service. IFR flights are separated from other IFR 
flights and receive traffic information in respect of VFR flights. 
VFR flights receive traffic information in respect of all other 
flights. 
Class E 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. IFR flights are provided with 
air traffic control service and are separated from other IFR 
flights. All flights receive traffic information as far as is practical. 
Class E shall not be used for control zones. 
Class F 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All participating IFR flights 
receive air traffic advisory service and all flights receive flight 
information service if requested. 
Class G 
IFR and VFR flights are permitted and receive flight information 
services if requested. 
Table 3-1. ATS Airspace Classes  
 
Controllers shall note that where airspaces under different classifications adjoin 
vertically, that is, one above the other, flights at a common level would comply with 
the requirements of and be given services applicable to the less restrictive class 
of airspace. In applying this criterion, Class B airspace shall therefore be 
considered less restrictive than Class A airspace, Class C airspace less restrictive 
than Class B airspace, etc. 
 
Controllers shall refer to the AIP for the designation and classification of airspace 
within the FIRs. 
 
The requirements for flights within each class of airspace are shown in Table 3-2.

Control Areas (CTAs) 
 
Control areas including, inter alia, airways are established to encompass sufficient 
airspace to contain the flight paths of those IFR flights or portions thereof to which 
it is desired to provide the applicable parts of the air traffic control service, taking 
into account the capabilities of the navigation aids normally used in that area. 
CTAs usually consist of Terminal Control Area (TMA), Control Zone (CTR) and 
Aerodrome Traffic Zone (ATZ). 
 
A lower limit of CTAs shall be established: 
 At a height above the ground or water of not less than 700 ft; 
 When practicable and desirable in order to allow freedom of action for VFR 
flights below the control area, be established at a greater height than the 
minimum specified in a). 
 
When the lower limit of a CTA is above 3,000 ft MSL, it should coincide with a 
VFR cruising level of the tables in Table 7-2 and Table 7-3. 
Note. -  This implies that the selected VFR cruising level be such that expected 
local atmospheric pressure variations do not result in a lowering of this limit to 
a height of less than 700 ft above ground or water. 
 
An upper limit of a CTA shall be established when either: 
 Air traffic control service will not be provided above such upper limit; or 
 The CTA is situated below an upper CTA, in which case, the upper limit shall

a height of less than 700 ft above ground or water.

CTAs shall be determined in accordance with ICAO PANS-OPS.

delineated to include the upper airspace within the lateral limits of a number of 
lower FIRs or CTAs.

General 
 
Notwithstanding the designation of an airspace for a specific purpose, certain 
activities may require the temporary release of airspace by one controlling 
authority to the other for specific periods. Such release of airspace shall be 
undertaken by the airspace reservation or block clearance systems described 
herein. 
4.2 
Distinction Between the Block Clearance and Airspace Reservation Systems 
 
A block clearance is an authorisation by a controlling authority for the release of 
airspace, or a defined portion thereof, to another controlling authority for a 
significant period of time to permit aircraft to usefully utilise that airspace.  
 
Examples of circumstances that would require the issue of a block clearance are 
given below: 
 When a military-restricted area is being used by limited military aircraft, which 
will permit other aircraft operations to be confined to agreed sectors or 
geographical areas or height bands within that area; and 
 In civil control areas, civil traffic may be required to confine their operations to 
agreed flight levels or make minor diversions to permit passage of military 
aircraft.

General 
 
Restrictions of varying degrees of severity are necessary to accommodate the 
requirements of certain activities, which are not compatible with civil aviation, 
example ground to air firing. In addition, there are also aerial activities by specific 
users or user groups which may require the reservation of portions of airspace for 
their exclusive use for determined periods of time, example military air exercises.

other users, it is the responsibility of the user requesting for such restrictions or 
reservations to consider and determine the following: 
 Whether the activities leading to the request for the establishment of an 
airspace restriction or reservation are in fact valid and justified; and 
 The minimum needs, in terms of space, time and conditions of use, required 
to confine the activities so that potential hazards and disruptions to other users 
of the airspace are minimised or avoided. 
 
Following the request by the user, the CAAM and the military shall confer and 
reach agreement for the establishment of restricted or reservation of airspace. The 
publication of the details of the airspace shall be published in accordance with 
normal procedures.

Special VFR Flights 
 
A Special VFR flight is a VFR flight cleared by air traffic control to operate within a 
control zone in meteorological conditions below VMC or between the hours of 
sunset and sunrise. Special VFR is intended to afford greater freedom of 
movement to pilots who are unable to comply with IFR. Special VFR flights may

traffic conditions, the extent of the proposed flight and the availability of air-to-
ground communications.

instruct the Special VFR aircraft to fly not above a certain level. Standard 
separation must be provided between all special VFR flights and, between Special 
VFR flights and IFR flights. The aircraft must be capable of two-way radio

8.1 
General 
 
The continuity of Reduced Vertical Separation Minima (RVSM) operations safely 
in relation to the provision of air navigation services requires that ATC procedures 
be periodically reviewed and appropriate recurrent training provided. As a basis 
for the periodic review of regional procedures, consideration should be given to 
the appropriate action to be taken by controllers in the following situations, as 
applicable: 
 Aircraft known not to be suitably equipped are flight-planned into RVSM 
airspace; 
 An aircraft informs ATC that the capability to maintain a Cleared Flight Level 
(CFL) appropriate to RVSM requirements has been lost; 
 
The pilot advises that the automatic altitude-keeping device has been turned 
off, and 
 The displayed altitude differs from the CFL by 300 ft or more. 
Note1. - While not necessary to support RVSM operations, the availability of 
altitude display is beneficial.

9.1 
Objectives 
 
Air traffic service is a generic term encompassing air traffic control service, flight 
information service, alerting service and air traffic advisory service. Air traffic 
advisory service however is not provided within Malaysia FIRs. 
 
The objectives of the air traffic services are to: 
 Prevent collisions between aircraft; 
 Prevent collisions between aircraft on the manoeuvring area and obstructions 
on that area; 
 
Expedite and maintain an orderly flow of air traffic; 
 Provide advice and information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of 
flights; and 
 Notify appropriate organisations regarding aircraft in need of search and 
rescue aid, and assist such organisations as required. 
9.2 
Divisions of The Air Traffic Services 
 
In providing air traffic services, controllers shall bear in mind that their primary 
responsibility is to prevent collisions. Traffic expedition, although important, must 
never take precedence over their primary responsibility. 
 
The air traffic services comprise three identifiable services as follows: 
 Air traffic control service to achieve the objectives a), b) and c) of paragraph 
9.1.2; 
 Flight information service to achieve d) in paragraph 9.1.2; and 
 
Alerting service to achieve objective e) in paragraph 9.1.2.

The provision of air traffic services shall be determined by consideration of the 
following: 
 The types of air traffic involved; 
 The density of air traffic;

whereas a relatively greater density of traffic where only one type of operation 
is involved would not;

is a constant flow of air traffic (e.g., scheduled traffic), whereas similar or worse 
meteorological conditions might be relatively unimportant in an area where air 
traffic would be discontinued in such conditions (e.g., local VFR flights); 
c) open stretches of water, mountainous, uninhabited or desert areas might 
necessitate the provision of air traffic services even though the frequency of

General 
 
The purpose of contingency plan is to provide a safe and orderly flow of domestic 
and international air traffic in the event of disruptions of air traffic services and 
related supporting services.

 Develop contingency plans for introduction in respect of generally foreseeable 
events such as industrial action or labour unrest affecting the air traffic 
services and or supporting services; and  
 Monitor any developments which might lead to events requiring contingency 
measures to be applied. 
 
When determining the level of services to be provided under the contingency plan, 
the following shall be considered:  
 Airspace management; 
 Traffic densities; 
 
Complexity of airspace arrangements and pilot/ATC procedures; 
 Special operations such as: 
1) Aircraft emergencies; 
2) Search and rescue and mercy flights; 
3) Military operations; 
 Foreign state aircraft which have already been given diplomatic approval; 
 
En route international flights and 
 The alternate level of personnel, services and facilities available.

traffic services to another ATSU. Accordingly, letters of agreement stating the 
notification procedure, responsibilities and other details for the transfer of

Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe

The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

CAAM recognise that fatigue affects a person’s health and well-being, increase

reasonable, workplace fatigue and its risks, to ensure a safe and error-free work 
environment for employees, contractors and clients. The objectives of the Fatigue

 Controllers are fit for work; 
 The organisation enjoys a safe working environment by minimising hazards 
associated with fatigue; 
 
The fatigue hazards associated with long work hours and shift works are 
minimised; 
 All personnel have access to gain assistance through a range of preventative 
initiatives, including training; 
 Informed or joint decisions are to be made regarding work design; 
 
On-going risk assessment and hazard monitoring takes place; and 
 Employees unfit for duty as a result of fatigue will be dealt with consistently 
and fairly.

If the request is being approved, OCC unit shall forward the approval to the 
corresponding air operators; and  
 If the request is not approved, the Regional Director/Deputy Director 
Operations and ATS Airport Manager will state the reason for non-approval 
and OCC unit shall forward the reason to the corresponding air operators.  
 
Extension requests not approved after aircraft departed the aerodrome of 
departure:   
 If an aircraft has departed the aerodrome of departure, OCC unit shall 
inform the ATCC Watch Manager that the requested extension at the 
arrival aerodrome is not approved and request for the aircraft’s intended 
action; and  
 OCC unit shall communicate the aircraft’s intended action to both departing 
and arrival aerodrome.  
 
Request not approved prior to aircraft departure from the aerodrome of 
departure.  
 If an aircraft has yet to departed, OCC unit shall contact the ATSU at the 
aerodrome of departure to advise that extension request at the arrival 
aerodrome is not approved and to obtain the aircraft’s intended action; and

Introduction 
 
This Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1 is one of a series of Air Navigation 
Services Manual (ANSM) issued by the Air Navigation Services Divisions (ANSD) and 
designed to serve as a reference for employees of ANSD responsible for promoting the safe 
and orderly development of international civil aviation.  It is a comprehensive manual that 
provides guidance and standards for the provision of air traffic services. The ANSM is ANSD 
internal document. This manual is published pursuant to Regulation 154 of Civil Aviation 
Regulations 2016. This document is officially designated as ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1. 
The ANSM 9 - MATS Volume 1 is an important reference for air traffic controllers to ensure 
the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective. 
Throughout this MATS Volume 1, the use of masculine pronouns should be understood to 
represent male and female persons. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(Dato’ Captain Norazman Bin Mahmud) 
Chief Executive Officer 
Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia

General 
1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 19 - Search and Rescue 
(SAR), Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 2026. 
 
The contents of this, MATS Volume 1 Part 19 - Search and Rescue (SAR) shall 
be read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 11, CAD 1101, CAD 12, 
International Civil Aviation Organization Doc 9731 and ANSM 5 - Aeronautical 
Search and Rescue Manual. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1 Part 19 - Search and Rescue (SAR) contains standard 
operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers and other 
operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their 
area of responsibility. 
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026. 
1.4 
Interpretation of Words 
Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788]. 
May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative. 
Miles always refers to nautical miles (NM). 
Shall, is to, are to and must means the instruction is mandatory.

Search and Rescue System 
2.1 
Introduction 
 
Aeronautical Search and Rescue (SAR) is broadly defined as the search for 
aircraft in distress (or referred to as an “aeronautical incident”) and the provision 
of aid to persons who are, or feared to be, in need of assistance, regardless of the 
nationality or status of such persons or the circumstances in which such persons 
are found, whether it occurs over land or sea. 
 
Aeronautical SAR services in Malaysia are provided by the Civil Aviation Authority 
of Malaysia (CAAM), as the Lead SAR Authority in collaboration with the 
Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA), Royal Military Air Force 
(RMAF), Royal Malaysian Navy (RMN), Royal Malaysia Police (RMP), Marine 
Department and Fire and Rescue Department Malaysia. 
 
The services are available on a 24-hour basis by the provisions stipulated in CAD 
12 - Search and Rescue. The International Aeronautical and Maritime SAR 
Manual (IAMSAR Manual) ICAO Doc 9731: Vol. I, II and III are the reference 
documents for the international requirements.

2.2 
CAAM SAR and Disaster Management Objective 
Note. - See ANSM 5 – ASARM, Chapter 3, Para 3.1. for CAAM SAR and Disaster 
Management Objective. 
 
CAAM’s objectives for SAR and Disaster Management within Malaysia are as 
follows:  
 Support the National SAR Committee's objectives and implement Malaysia's 
Aeronautical SAR Policy issued by the National Security Council through 2 
core activities: SAR Operations and Prevention; 
 Determine Malaysia's Aeronautical SAR policies and practices in line with 
International Civil Aviation Organisation and International requirement; 
 
Provide and coordinate SAR services for aircraft in distress within the Kuala 
Lumpur and Kota Kinabalu Search and Rescue Regions (SRRs) and in other 
areas as permitted by the Minister; and 
 When applicable, support and assist disaster management activities and 
operations at District, State, and National levels.

CAAM SAR’s Responsibility 
Note. - See ANSM 5 – ASARM, Chapter 3, Para 3.2 for CAAM SAR Responsibilities. 
 
CAAM SAR is responsible for: 
 Overall coordination of SAR for any aeronautical incidents involving aircraft 
that occurs over water, air and/or land, within Kuala Lumpur and Kota 
Kinabalu SRRs, the boundaries of which coincide with the Kuala Lumpur and 
Kota Kinabalu Flight Information Regions, with the following exception of: 
1) Urban/populated and built-up areas that requires emergency and disaster 
response, the National Security Council, Directive No 20 prevails;  
2) Within a 5 NM (8 kilometres) radius of an airport/aerodrome where the 
local Airport Emergency Plan (AEP) prevail;  
3) Military aircraft, where RMAF conducts the A-SAR mission, with 
assistance from CAAM; and 
4) Border areas of Malaysia/Indonesia where the SAR Manual of 
Malaysia/Indonesia by the General Border Committee prevails. 
 Supporting disaster relief operations, if required, in the event of any disaster 
incident.

ARCC/ARSC, which operates on a 24-hour basis. SAR Chief's responsibility is

 SAR Chief of Peninsular; Deputy Director of KL ATCC; 
 SAR Chief of Sabah; Deputy Director (Operations) Sabah; and 
 
SAR Chief of Sarawak; Deputy Director (Operations) Sarawak.

RCC Support Staff is an air traffic controller who had successfully attended the

 In the event of SAR operations, assigned in the SMC Team to perform duties

the safe and efficient operation of air traffic services. It is updated periodically to reflect the 
latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 11, CAD 1101, International Civil

operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services under their 
area of responsibility.

context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller.

Overview 
2.1 
General 
 
ATS units (ATSUs) shall ensure that the level of Air Traffic Services (ATS) and 
Communication, Navigation and Surveillance (CNS), as well as the ATS 
procedures applicable to the airspace or aerodrome concerned, are appropriate 
and adequate for maintaining an acceptable level of safety in the provision of ATS. 
 
The requirements in respect of services, systems and procedures applicable to 
airspaces and aerodromes should be established on the basis of a regional air 
navigation agreement in order to facilitate the harmonisation of ATS in adjacent 
airspaces. 
 
To ensure that safety in the provision of ATS is maintained, the Air Navigation 
Services Divisions (ANSD) shall implement Safety Management System (SMS) 
for the ATS under its jurisdiction. Where appropriate, ATS SMS should be 
established on the basis of a regional air navigation agreement. 
 
All ATSUs shall have in place a SMS acceptable to the Secretary General (Sec-
Gen) of the Ministry of Transport (MOT), which addresses high-level safety 
objectives as follows: 
a) Identify safety hazards; 
b) Safety risk management; 
c) Ensure the implementation of remedial action necessary to maintain agreed 
safety performance; 
d) Provide for continuous monitoring and regular assessment of the safety 
performance; and 
e) Aim at continuous improvement of the overall performance of the SMS.

5.1 
Collection and Evaluation of Safety-Related Data 
 
Data for use in safety monitoring programmes should be collected from as wide a 
range of sources as possible, as the safety-related consequences of particular 
procedures or systems may not be realised until after an incident has occurred. 
 
ANSD should establish a formal incident reporting system for ATS personnel to 
facilitate the collection of information on actual or potential safety hazards or 
deficiencies related to the provision of ATS, including route structures, procedures, 
CNS systems and other safety significant systems and equipment as well as 
controller workloads. 
Note. - Guidance related to both mandatory and voluntary State incident reporting 
systems is contained in the Safety Management Manual (ICAO Doc 9859) and 
CAD 1900.

incident reports, shall be systematically reviewed by ANSD in order to detect any

principles.

Capacity Management  
2.1 
General  
 
The capacity of an Air Traffic Services (ATS) system depends on many factors, 
including the ATS route structure, the navigation accuracy of the aircraft using the 
airspace, weather-related factors, and controller workload. Every effort should be 
made to provide sufficient capacity to cater to both normal and peak traffic levels; 
however, in implementing any measures to increase capacity, Air Navigation 
Services Divisions (ANSD) shall ensure, in accordance with the procedures 
specified relating safety levels are not jeopardised.  
 
The number of aircraft provided with an Air Traffic Control (ATC) service shall not 
exceed that which can be safely handled by the ATC unit concerned under the 
prevailing circumstances. In order to define the maximum number of flights which 
can be safely accommodated, ANSD should assess and declare the ATC capacity 
for control areas, for control sectors within a control area and for aerodromes.  
 
ATC capacity should be expressed as the maximum number of aircraft which can 
be accepted over a given period of time within the airspace or at the aerodrome 
concerned.  
Note. - The most appropriate measure of capacity is likely to be the sustainable 
hourly traffic flow. Such hourly capacities can, for example, be converted into daily, 
monthly or annual values.

Chapter 3 - Air Traffic Flow Management 
 
 
 
3-1 
3 
Air Traffic Flow Management 
3.1 
General  
 
Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) service shall be implemented for airspace 
where traffic demand at times exceeds the defined ATC capacity.  
 
ATFM should be implemented on the basis of a regional air navigation agreement 
or, when appropriate, as a multilateral agreement.  
 
The ATFM service within a region or other defined area, should be developed and 
implemented as a centralised ATFM organisation, supported by flow management 
positions established at each Area Control Centre (ACC) within the region or area 
of applicability.  
 
Certain flights may be exempt from ATFM measures, or be given priority over other 
flights.  
 
Detailed procedures governing the provision of the ATFM measures, and service 
within a region or area should be prescribed in a regional ATFM manual or 
handbook. 
3.2 
Flow Management Procedures  
 
ATFM should be carried out in three phases:  
 Strategic planning, if the action is carried out more than one day before the 
day on which it will take effect. Strategic planning is normally carried out well 
in advance, typically two to six months ahead;  
 Pre-tactical planning, if the action is to be taken on the day before the day on 
which it will take effect; and 
 
Tactical operations, if the action is taken on the day on which it will take effect.  
3.3 
Strategic Planning

3.3 
Strategic Planning  
 
Strategic planning should be carried out in conjunction with ATC and the aircraft 
operators. It should consist of examining the demand for the forthcoming season, 
assessing where and when demand is likely to exceed the available ATC capacity 
and taking steps to resolve the imbalance by:  
 Arranging with the ATC authority to provide adequate capacity at the required 
place and time;  
 Rerouting certain traffic flows (traffic orientation);  
 
Scheduling or rescheduling flights as appropriate; and

General 
1.1 
Citation 
 
The Manual of Air Traffic Services (MATS) Volume 1, Part 4 - General Provisions 
for Air Traffic Services, Issue 02/Revision 02, comes into operation on 03 July 
2026. 
 
The contents of this MATS Volume 1, Part 4 - General Provisions for Air Traffic 
Services shall be read together with Civil Aviation Directive (CAD) 3, CAD 10, CAD 
11, CAD 15, CAD 1101, International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Doc 7030, 
ICAO Doc 8168, ICAO Doc 8643, ICAO Doc 8896, ICAO Doc 9426, ICAO Doc 
4444, ICAO Doc 10037 and ICAO Doc 10122. 
1.2 
Applicability 
 
The MATS Volume 1, Part 4 - General Provisions for Air Traffic Services contains 
standard operating procedures, act as guidance material for air traffic controllers 
and other operational personnel tasked with the provision of air traffic services 
under their area of responsibility.  
 
The term of Air Traffic Controller and Controller being used interchangeably in the 
context of this manual means Air Traffic Controller. 
1.3 
Revocation 
 
This ANSM 9 Issue 02 Revision 02 revokes Air Navigation Services Manual 9 
dated 09 January 2026. 
1.4 
Interpretation of Words 
Authority means the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia established under the Civil 
Aviation Authority of Malaysia Act 2017 [Act 788]. 
May means the procedure/instruction is permissive, optional or alternative.

Responsibility for the Provision of ATC Service 
2.1 
Area Control Service 
 
Area control service shall be provided:  
 By an Area Control Centre (ACC); or 
 By the unit providing approach control service in a Control Zone (CTR) or in 
a Control Area (CTA) of limited extent which is designated primarily for the 
provision of approach control service, when no ACC is established. 
2.2 
Approach Control Service  
 
Approach control service shall be provided:   
 By an aerodrome control tower or an ACC, when it is necessary or desirable 
to combine under the responsibility of one unit the functions of the approach 
control service and those of the aerodrome control service or the area control 
service; or  
 By an approach control unit, when it is necessary or desirable to establish a 
separate unit.  
Note. - Approach control service may be provided by a unit collocated with an 
ACC, or by a control sector within an ACC. 
2.3 
Aerodrome Control Service  
 
Aerodrome control service shall be provided by an aerodrome control tower.   
Note. - The task of providing specified services on the apron, e.g., apron 
management service, may be assigned to an aerodrome control tower or to a 
separate unit.

Division of Responsibility for Control Between ATC Units   
4.1 
General  
 
The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) shall designate the area of responsibility for 
each Air Traffic Services Unit (ATSU) and, when applicable, for individual control 
sectors within an ATSU. Where there is more than one ATC working position within 
a unit or sector, the duties and responsibilities of the individual working positions 
shall be defined.  
4.2 
Between a Unit Providing Aerodrome Control Service and a Unit Providing 
Approach Control Service  
 
Except for flights which are provided by aerodrome control service only, the control 
of arriving and departing controlled flights shall be divided between units providing 
aerodrome control service and units providing approach control service as follows:  
 
Arriving aircraft. Control of an arriving aircraft shall be transferred from the unit 
providing approach control service to the unit providing aerodrome control 
service when the aircraft:  
 Is in the vicinity of the aerodrome, and  
 it is considered that approach and landing will be completed in visual 
reference to the ground, or  
 has reached uninterrupted visual meteorological conditions, or  
 Is at a prescribed point or level, or  
 
Has landed, as specified in letters of agreement or ATSU instructions.

5.1 
Flight Plan Form  
 
A flight plan form based on the model in Part 11 - Air Traffic Services Messages 
should be provided and should be used by operators and ATSU for the purpose 
of completing flight plans. Information relative to an intended flight or portion of a 
flight, to be provided to ATSUs, shall be in the form of a flight plan.  
 
The flight plan form should be printed in English.  
 
Operators and ATSU should comply with:  
 The instructions for completion of the flight plan form given in Part 11 - Air 
Traffic Services Messages; and  
 Any constraints identified in relevant Aeronautical Information Publication 
(AIP) Malaysia.  
Note1. - Failure to adhere to the provisions in paragraph 5.1.3 a) or any constraint 
identified in relevant AIPs may result in data being rejected, processed incorrectly 
or lost.  
Note2. - The instructions for completing the flight plan form given as paragraph 
5.1.3 a) may be conveniently printed on the inside cover of flight plan form pads, 
or posted in briefing rooms.  
 
The flight plan shall be submitted by the operator or pilot-in-command at least 180 
minutes prior to estimated off-block time (EOBT) for the following: 
 Flights departing from Malaysian airports whose destinations are outside 
Malaysia. 
 Flights departing from Peninsular Malaysia airports for Sabah/Sarawak and 
vice versa.

6.1 
Scope and Purpose  
 
Clearances are issued solely for expediting and separating air traffic and are 
based on known traffic conditions which affect safety in aircraft operation. Such 
traffic conditions include not only aircraft in the air and on the manoeuvring area 
over which control is being exercised, but also any vehicular traffic or other 
obstructions not permanently installed on the manoeuvring area in use.  
 
If an ATC clearance is not suitable for the pilot-in-command of an aircraft, the flight 
crew may request and, if practicable, obtain an amended clearance.  
 
The issuance of ATC clearances by ATSUs constitutes authority for an aircraft to 
proceed only in so far as known air traffic is concerned. ATC clearances do not 
constitute authority to violate any applicable regulations for promoting the safety 
of flight operations or for any other purpose; neither do clearances relieve a pilot-
in-command of any responsibility whatsoever in connection with a possible 
violation of applicable rules and regulations.  
 
ATSUs shall issue such ATC clearances as are necessary to prevent collisions 
and to expedite and maintain an orderly flow of air traffic.  
 
ATC clearances must be issued early enough to ensure that they are transmitted 
to the aircraft in sufficient time for it to comply with them.

General  
 
In order to facilitate a safe and orderly flow of traffic, aircraft may, subject to

Speed control shall not be applied to aircraft entering or established in a holding 
pattern.  
 
Speed adjustments should be limited to those necessary to establish and/or

The flight crew shall inform the ATSU concerned if at any time they are unable to

13.1 
General 
 
When operational and/or routine meteorological information is to be reported, 
using data link, by an aircraft en route at times where position reports are required 
in accordance with paragraph 12.1.1 and paragraph 12.1.2, the position report 
shall be given in accordance with paragraph 12.5.2 (requirements concerning 
transmission of meteorological information from ADS-C equipped aircraft), or in 
the form of a routine air-report. Special aircraft observations shall be reported as 
special air-reports. All air-reports shall be reported as soon as is practicable. 
13.2 
Contents of Routine Air-Reports 
 
Routine air-reports transmitted by data link, when ADS-C is not being applied, 
shall give information relating to such of the following elements as are necessary 
for compliance with paragraph 13.2.2: 
Section 1. Position information: 
 Aircraft identification 
 Position 
 
Time 
 Flight level or altitude 
 Next position and time over 
 
Ensuing significant point 
Section 2. Operational information: 
 Estimated time of arrival 
 Endurance 
Section 3. Meteorological information: 
 
Wind direction 
 
Wind speed 
 
Wind quality flag 
 
Air temperature 
 Turbulence (if available) 
 Humidity (if available).

Volcanic Activity  
 
Emissions during a volcanic activity have serious impact on the safety of aircraft 
operations and therefore information on volcanic activity must be disseminated 
without delay to pilots and airline operators.  
 
The Air Traffic Control Centre upon receiving information on volcanic activity that 
is likely to affect international routes shall take the following actions:  
 Notify aircraft that are likely to be affected;  
 Report the information immediately to the meteorological office;  
 
Issue a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) giving details of such activity;  
 Coordinate with the airline representatives and the ATS agencies of 
neighbouring States to implement contingency routes to bypass the area likely 
to be affected by the volcanic emissions; and  
 Record in the ATS log of the activity and actions taken.  
 
Details of the activity to be included in the NOTAM shall be as follows (see

Special air-reports containing observations of volcanic activity shall be recorded 
on the special air-report of volcanic activity form. Forms based on the model form

Forwarding of Meteorological Information 
 
When receiving ADS-C reports which contain a meteorological information block, 
ATSUs shall relay the basic ADS-C and meteorological information blocks and 
aircraft registration without delay to the World Area Forecast Centres (WAFCs). 
Note. - Specifications concerning the format to be used in the relay of 
meteorological information to the WAFCs are contained in the Manual on 
Aeronautical Meteorological Practice (ICAO Doc 8896). 
 
When receiving special air-reports by data link communications, ATSUs shall 
forward them without delay to their associated meteorological watch office, the 
WAFCs, and the centres designated by regional air navigation agreement for the 
operation of aeronautical fixed service Internet-based services.

General

coordination with adjacent ATSU and control sectors.

Application for The Purpose of Managing CNS Maintenance Contract

operation of CAAM CNS maintenance contracts by multiple vendors.

 Eliminate/Reduce Paperwork: to eliminate/reduce paperwork and clipboards 
by the system's ability to automatically capture the equipment information.  
 Web/Mobile Access: access to information on assets and maintenance data 
remotely via web browser and mobile application.  
 
System Inventory & Spares Management: minimising time in locating and 
tracking inventory & spares in multiple stations. 
 Preventive & Corrective Maintenance: providing maintenance schedule 
information for preventative maintenance and corrective maintenance 
requirements of the system.

Malfunction or Disruption Report Procedure 
 
ATC shall carry out the following procedures to assist the MET Malaysia in 
identifying the issue and determining the root cause of the equipment or system 
malfunction/disruption prior to any corrective action being undertaken:  
 Conduct Preliminary Diagnostics 
 ATC personnel shall perform an initial diagnostic assessment to 
identify the root cause of any malfunction or disruption affecting 
meteorological systems or equipment; 
Note. - See para 15.43.2 for identifying malfunctions or disruptions. 
 Initiate Prompt Corrective Measures 
 If the issue is minor and within ATC’s capacity to resolve, immediate 
corrective action should be taken prior to submitting a formal fault 
report; 
Note. - See para 15.4.3.3 for initial corrective actions to be undertaken by ATC.

followed up with a phone call to ensure receipt and to expedite further

 Document Feedback and Coordinate Further Action 
 ATC shall document all feedback received from the Meteorological 
Office/Station and coordinate necessary follow-up measures, 
including the issuance of NOTAMs, AIP Supplements, or AIP 
Amendments, where applicable. 
 
ATC shall identify malfunctions or disruptions based on the following indicators: 
 Disruption in radar image display and Wind Shear alerts is typically 
attributed to a malfunction in the Wind Shear Detection System (WSDS); 
 Disruption in Wind and Runway Visual Range (WRVR) data display on the 
ABT website indicates a potential fault in the WRVR system;

Data Link Communications Initiation Procedures 
16.1 
General 
Note1. - Provisions concerning the data link initiation capability (DLIC) are contained 
in CAD 10, Volume II, Chapter 8. 
Note2. - Guidance material relating to the implementation of DLIC can be found in 
the Global Operational Data Link (GOLD) Manual (ICAO Doc 10037). 
 
Before entering an airspace where data link applications are used by the ATSU, 
data link communications shall be initiated between the aircraft and the ATSU in 
order to register the aircraft and, when necessary, allow the start of a data link 
application. This shall be initiated by the aircraft, either automatically or by the 
pilot, or by the ATSU on address forwarding. 
 
The logon address associated with an ATSU shall be published in AIP Malaysia 
in accordance with CAD 15. 
Note. - A given FIR may have multiple logon addresses; and more than one FIR 
may share the same logon address. 
16.2 
Aircraft Initiation 
 
On receipt of a valid data link initiation request from an aircraft approaching or 
within a data link service area, the ATSU shall accept the request and, if able to 
correlate it with a flight plan, shall establish a connection with the aircraft.

Failure 
 
In the case of a data link initiation failure, the data link system shall provide an 
indication of the failure to the appropriate ATSU(s). The data link system shall also 
provide an indication of the failure to the flight crew when a data link initiation 
failure results from a logon initiated by the flight crew. 
Note. - When the aircraft’s logon request results from responding to a contact 
request by a transferring ATSU, then both ATSUs will receive the indication.

shall be transmitted immediately after the departure of an aircraft for which the basic flight plan 
data have been previously distributed. The DEP message shall be created and transmitted in

FPL system) will be displayed. Click on any flight plans that you wish to create a DEP 
message for.

5. MONITORING FLIGHT MOVEMENTS 
 
ATCOs play a critical role in monitoring and managing flight movements from the moment a 
flight plan is filed, through all phases of the flight, including departure and arrival. The process 
begins with filing a flight plan, which contains key details such as the intended route, altitude, 
and estimated time of departure. Once the flight plan is filed, ATCOs ensures that the flight is 
scheduled and that any delays are communicated appropriately to avoid congestion in 
airspace or at airports. 
 
Upon departure, a DEP message is generated and sent by ATCOs to indicate that the aircraft 
has taken off. This message confirms that the flight has commenced and updates relevant 
stakeholders about the aircraft’s status. ATCOs continue to monitor the aircraft's progress 
throughout the flight, providing instructions and updates as necessary. 
 
Finally, upon arrival, an ARR message is created to indicate that the flight has landed 
successfully. This message marks the completion of the flight and updates the system to 
reflect that the aircraft has arrived at its destination. Throughout this process, ATCOs ensure 
that all phases of flight are coordinated smoothly, promoting safe and efficient air traffic 
management.

2.1 
Introduction 
 
In addition to the circumstances mentioned in Part 5, Chapter 12 - Reduction in 
Separation Minima, the separation minima detailed in Part 5, Chapter 5.1 - Lateral 
Separation and Chapter 5.2 - Longitudinal Separation, may be reduced in the 
vicinity of aerodromes if: 
 Adequate separation can be provided by the aerodrome controller when each 
aircraft is continuously visible to the controller; or  
 Each aircraft is continuously visible to flight crews of the other aircraft 
concerned and the pilots thereof report that they can maintain their own 
separation; or  
 
In the case of one aircraft following another, the flight crew of the succeeding 
aircraft reports that the other aircraft is in sight and separation can be 
maintained.

Procedures for Departing Aircraft 
4.1 
General 
 
Clearance for departing aircraft shall specify, when necessary for the separation 
of aircraft, direction of take-off and turn after take-off: heading or track to be made 
good before taking up the cleared departure track; level to maintain before 
continuing climb to assigned level; time, point and/or rate at which a level change 
shall be made; and any other necessary manoeuvre consistent with safe operation 
of the aircraft. 
 
At aerodromes where, Standard Instrument Departures (SIDs) have been 
established, departing aircraft should normally be cleared to follow the appropriate 
SID. 
 
The Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) service within a region or other defined 
area, should be developed and implemented as a centralised ATFM organisation, 
supported by flow management positions established at each Area Control Centre 
(ACC) within the region or area of applicability.  
 
Certain flights may be exempt from ATFM measures, or be given priority over other 
flights.  
 
Detailed procedures governing the provision of the ATFM measures, and service 
within a region or area should be prescribed in a regional ATFM manual or 
handbook.

Standard Clearances for Departing Aircraft 
 
General 
 
The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) should, wherever possible, establish 
standardised procedures for the transfer of control between the Air Traffic 
Services Units (ATSUs) concerned and standard clearances for departing 
aircraft. 
Note. - The provisions applying to standardised procedures for coordination 
and transfer of control are specified in Part 10, Chapter 2.  
 
Coordination 
 
 Where standard clearances for departing aircraft have been agreed to between 
the units concerned, the aerodrome control tower will normally issue the 
appropriate standard clearance without prior coordination with or approval from 
the approach control unit or ACC. 
 
Prior coordination of clearances should be required only in the event that a 
variation to the standard clearance or the standardised transfer of control 
procedures is necessary or desirable for operational reasons.

Functions of Aerodrome Control Towers 
2.1 
General 
 
Aerodrome control towers shall issue information and clearances to aircraft under 
their control to achieve a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of air traffic on and in 
the vicinity of an aerodrome with the object of preventing collision(s) between: 
 Aircraft flying within the designated area of responsibility of the control tower, 
including the aerodrome traffic circuits;  
 Aircraft operating on the manoeuvring area;  
 
Aircraft landing and taking off;  
 Aircraft and vehicles operating on the manoeuvring area; and 
 Aircraft on the manoeuvring area and obstructions on that area. 
 
Aerodrome controllers shall maintain a continuous watch on all flight operations 
on and in the vicinity of an aerodrome as well as vehicles and personnel on the 
manoeuvring area. Watch shall be maintained by visual observation, augmented 
when available by an Air Traffic Services (ATS) surveillance system. Traffic shall 
be controlled in accordance with the procedures set forth herein and all applicable 
traffic rules specified by the Chief Executive Officer (CEO). If there are other 
aerodromes within a control zone, traffic at all aerodromes within such a zone shall 
be coordinated so that traffic circuits do not conflict.

Visual observation shall be achieved through direct out-of-the-window

Automatic Recording of Surveillance Data 
 
Surveillance data from primary and secondary radar equipment or other 
systems [e.g., Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast (ADS-B), 
Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Contract (ADS-C)], used as an aid to air 
traffic services, shall be automatically recorded for use in accident and incident 
investigations, search and rescue, Air Traffic Control (ATC) and surveillance 
systems evaluation and training.

the recordings are pertinent to accident and incident investigations, they shall 
be retained for longer periods until it is evident that they will no longer be 
required.

latest developments in air traffic management and to ensure that it remains relevant and 
effective.

information other than that pertaining to the provision of air traffic control service.

uncertainty or the alert phase, it shall, when practicable, advise the operator prior 
to notifying the rescue coordination centre. 
Note. - If an aircraft is in the distress phase, the rescue coordination centre has to 
be notified immediately in accordance with 3.2.1. 
 
All information notified to the RCC by an area control or flight information centre 
shall, whenever practicable, also be communicated, without delay, to the operator. 
3.6 
Information to Aircraft in the Vicinity of an Aircraft in a State of Emergency 
 
When it has been established by an ATSU that an aircraft is in a state of 
emergency, other aircraft known to be in the vicinity of the aircraft involved shall, 
except as provided in 3.6.2, be informed of the nature of the emergency as soon 
as practicable.
